people.name: Jon Ossoff
people.background: Incumbent U.S. senator, in office since January 20, 2021 after winning the January 5, 2021 runoff. Born in Atlanta in 1987; bachelor's from Georgetown's School of Foreign Service (2009) and master's from the London School of Economics (2013). Before the Senate he was a national-security and legislative aide to U.S. Rep. Hank Johnson and then CEO of Insight TWI, a documentary company; he lost a high-profile 2017 special election for Georgia's 6th congressional district. In 2025–26 he sits on Appropriations (ranking member, Military Construction–VA subcommittee), Rules and Administration, and the Select Committee on Intelligence. He was unopposed in the May 19, 2026 Democratic primary.
people.ideology: Mainstream Democrat who stresses building a 'bipartisan coalition' and is a sharp critic of the Trump administration: one of 12 Senate Democrats to vote for the Laken Riley Act (2025), endorsed by Sierra Club Georgia and MoveOn as well as former Republican Sen. Jeff Flake and two Republican South Georgia mayors; Club for Growth Foundation lifetime score 2%.

positions.stance: Supports the Affordable Care Act, tried to restore the enhanced ACA premium tax credits, and opposed the 2025 reconciliation law's Medicaid changes (which he puts at about $1 trillion over a decade). Secured federal incentives meant to encourage Georgia to expand Medicaid and backed the $35 monthly insulin cap for Medicare recipients.

Opposes the 2025 Trump tax-and-spending law (H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act), arguing its tax cuts went predominantly to the wealthy and corporations and are outweighed by about $1 trillion in Medicaid reductions over a decade; has proposed tax cuts and incentives for small businesses and farmers and helped pass an expansion of the child tax credit.

Opposes Trump's tariffs, arguing a trade war amounts to taxes on consumers that damages Georgia industries; cites the bipartisan infrastructure law and federal manufacturing incentives as job drivers. Has made affordability a central 2026 campaign theme, arguing the Iran war adds pressure to household budgets alongside tariffs and health-care costs.

Supports secure borders and 'humane treatment,' backs deporting people in the country illegally who commit crimes, and was one of 12 Senate Democrats to vote for the 2025 Laken Riley Act. Has since sharply criticized Trump's immigration raids and how the law is enforced, pointing to more than 1,000 instances of human rights abuses in immigration detention facilities identified by his office's investigations.
Supports federal protections for abortion rights ('reproductive freedom') and has repeatedly condemned Georgia's 2019 six-week law; Planned Parenthood Action Fund endorsed him in 2020.

Reintroduced the Right to Vote Act in 2026 to create a federal statutory right to vote; rejects claims that the 2020 election was stolen and criticized the January 2026 FBI raid on Fulton County's election office as an effort to suppress Black votes.
Launched an investigation into large corporations and out-of-state landlords buying homes in bulk in Georgia and backed bipartisan legislation on institutional investors buying single-family homes.

positions.topic: Energy and utility bills / data centers
positions.stance: Opened an investigation into whether data-center growth is raising household electricity bills and warned federal regulators that costs could be shifted onto households; has not called for a moratorium.
Pushed to make Pell Grants available for shorter-term training, backed the bipartisan JOBS Act and directed federal money to technical colleges, universities, workforce programs and HBCUs.

Opposes the U.S.–Israeli war with Iran as a 'regime change war-of-choice' that began without congressional authorization; says he firmly supports efforts to safeguard Israel's security but has voted several times to halt specific arms transfers, citing the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.
Introduced legislation to ban corporate PACs and is pushing a congressional stock-trading ban that he says cleared a major Senate committee for the first time (2026).

Runs as a critic of the Trump administration, saying in May 2026 that the midterms require 'opposition' and 'the restoration of checks and balances'; branded Trump-backed measures — $1 billion in security funding tied to a new White House ballroom and a $1.8 billion fund for people who say they were politically persecuted — a 'crooked ballroom' and a 'slush fund' for Jan. 6 rioters.

Ranking Democrat on the Appropriations subcommittee on Military Construction–VA; pursued facility upgrades, rural transportation and funding for a veterans cemetery near Augusta; voted for the 2022 PACT Act.

Bipartisan law with Sen. Blackburn will toughen penalties on websites and social media companies failing to report crimes against children; supports bipartisan bill to protect children from online sexual abuse and exploitation; supports bipartisan law to hold tech companies accountable for child sex abuse material.
q: Sen. Ossoff’s bipartisan law with Sen. Marsha Blackburn will toughen penalties on websites and social media companies that fail to report crimes against children
Washington, D.C.— U.S. Senator Jon Ossoff’s bipartisan bill to protect children from online sexual abuse and exploitation is now law.

positions.stance: Flipped a dozen counties that backed Trump two years earlier.
q: Ossoff flipped a dozen counties that backed Trump two years earlier, including Lowndes County in South Georgia, where the Democrat won the endorsement of Valdosta’s GOP mayor.

positions.stance: Defended voting rights and civil rights at home.
q: That we defended voting rights and civil rights at home.

positions.stance: Pushed for a 70% cut to tariffs on U.S. pecan exports by the Republic of India.
q: In 2023,following Sen. Ossoff’s push, the Republic of India announced a major 70% cut to tariffs on U.S. pecan exports — helping growers sell more products

positions.stance: Would bring reckless and unnecessary war to an end.
q: We need to bring this reckless and unnecessary war to an end.

people.record: Voted for the 2022 PACT Act; one of 12 Senate Democrats voting for the Laken Riley Act (2025); opposed H.R. 1, the 2025 Trump tax-and-spending law; reintroduced the Right to Vote Act (2026); chaired the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations (2021–22) and Judiciary's Human Rights and the Law subcommittee (2023–24); has investigated foster-care and prison conditions, USPS failures and immigration detention; backed the $35 Medicare insulin cap.
endorsements: Republican mayors Scott James Matheson (Valdosta) and Julie Smith (Tifton), who said they plan to support him (reported Aug. 2026)

signals.claim: Would likely back restoring enhanced ACA premium subsidies and new federal incentives for holdout states to expand Medicaid if Democrats regain a majority.
signals.basis: He tried to restore the enhanced premium tax credits and secured federal Medicaid-expansion incentives for Georgia (AJC, Sept. 2026).

signals.claim: Would likely support federal limits on institutional-investor purchases of single-family homes.
signals.basis: Launched a Senate investigation into corporate and out-of-state buyers of homes and backed bipartisan legislation on institutional investors buying single-family homes (AJC, Sept. 2026).

signals.claim: May support federal rules requiring data centers to bear grid costs rather than residential ratepayers.
signals.basis: Opened an investigation into data centers and electricity bills and warned federal regulators that costs could shift to households; stopped short of a moratorium (AJC, Sept. 2026).

signals.claim: Would likely vote against funding or authorization for continued military operations against Iran.
signals.basis: Opposes the war as unauthorized and a 'war-of-choice' (AJC, Sept. 2026; Fox 5, Oct. 2026).

people.name: Mike Collins
people.background: U.S. representative for Georgia's 10th District since January 2023 (did not seek re-election in 2026); son of the late Rep. Mac Collins. Born in and lives in Jackson (Butts County); bachelor's from Georgia State University (1990). Spent his career in the family trucking business, Collins Trucking Company, and was Butts County Chamber president, an Associated Credit Union board chair and a Georgia Motor Trucking Association leader. Lost the 2014 GA-10 Republican runoff to Jody Hice. In the House he chairs the Transportation and Infrastructure subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment and serves on the Whip team. Won the May 19, 2026 Senate primary (40.5%) and the June 16 runoff over Derek Dooley, 55.5%–44.5%.
people.ideology: Trump-aligned 'America First' conservative who calls himself a 'conservative workhorse'; endorsed by President Trump, Gov. Brian Kemp, Club for Growth PAC (lifetime CfGF score 100%), Turning Point Action and CPAC; author of the Laken Riley Act and, per Roll Call, a prolific social media user whose posts on X have drawn criticism.

positions.stance: Voted for the 2025 Trump tax-and-spending law (H.R. 1), which included new tax breaks involving tips, overtime and older Americans, and portrays Ossoff's opposition to it as a vote for higher taxes; calls for a 'smaller, more accountable government,' citing excessive federal spending and fraud.

Blames the Affordable Care Act for rising costs and wants it repealed; supports price transparency and expanded health savings accounts; touts the $50 billion rural health fund in H.R. 1 and frames the law's Medicaid changes as anti-fraud.

Authored the Laken Riley Act — the first bill Trump signed in his second term (2025) — which provides for detaining immigrants without legal status who are charged with certain crimes; backs Trump's mass-deportation campaign and says illegal immigration strains housing, public services and taxpayer resources. Says the southern border is now secure.
Said in 2022 that he has 'always been and always will be 100% pro-life, period — no exceptions'; backs Georgia's 2019 six-week law and has opposed using federal money for abortions.

Has claimed Trump won Georgia in 2020 and called the result a 'federal hijacking' (the AJC describes the claim as false); cheered the January 2026 FBI raid on Fulton County's election office ('Go get 'em, Kash'); cosponsored the SAVE America Act requiring proof of citizenship to register for federal elections.

Blames limited supply and federal regulation for high costs; sponsored the PERMIT Act to speed environmental reviews and permitting and argues mass deportations would reduce housing demand; also cites lower interest rates.
Says the U.S. needs data centers to compete with China on AI and that the federal government should help ensure financing, while local communities should have the final say on siting.

Emphasizes alternatives to four-year degrees: backs the bipartisan Aviation Workforce Development Act, which would let families use 529 college-savings accounts for advanced pilot and maintenance training and other technical and career training, and calls for more resources for skilled trades and technical education; voted for the House GOP Parents Bill of Rights (H.R. 5, 2023).

Has repeatedly backed Trump's handling of the U.S.–Israeli war with Iran, calling the approach 'peace through strength,' and says Trump had the right to prevent Iran's leaders from acquiring a nuclear weapon; presents himself as 'an unequivocal supporter of Israel' and has voted repeatedly to fund Israeli missile defenses and weapons systems and to transfer arms to Israel.
Sponsored the VORTEX Act to improve sharing of veterans' opioid histories to prevent overprescribing; calls for more mental-health resources for veterans.
Backs Trump's tax cuts, deregulation and domestic-energy expansion as the route to lower prices, blames Biden-era spending for inflation, and wants to cut permitting and expand technical training.

Authored two laws signed by two different presidents, passed two bills into law under two presidents, authored two bills signed into law by two presidents of two different parties, and passed two pieces of legislation signed into law by two presidents from two different parties.
q: One of the only members of Congress who has ever actually passed anything, Collins authored two laws signed by two different presidents.

In just two years, Collins passed two bills into law under two presidents–the TRANQ Act and Laken Riley Act–and got it done the old fashion way: knocking on doors, listening to problems, and finding solutions.

positions.stance: Promised to fight to make sure no one would have to live through the pain of Laken Riley's murder, supports protecting borders, fighting crime, making life safer, more affordable, and more prosperous, and says fought to protect women, girls, and the most vulnerable in society.
q: When Laken Riley was murdered in Athens, Georgia by an illegal alien, Collins made a promise to the Riley family that he would fight to make sure that no one would have to live through their pain again.
That builds on a vision where the working man is forgotten no more, where we protect our borders and fight crime; where we make life safer, more affordable, and more prosperous.

positions.stance: Signed a bipartisan law to help law enforcement fight deadly drugs.
q: A bipartisan law signed by Biden to help law enforcement fight deadly drugs in our communities.

positions.stance: Would do exactly what he did as your next United States Senator.
q: And that is exactly what I will do every single day as your next United States Senator.

people.record: Author of the Laken Riley Act (2025; the first bill Trump signed in his second term) and, per his campaign, the TRANQ Act; voted for H.R. 1 (the 2025 tax-and-spending law) and H.R. 5 (Parents Bill of Rights, 2023); sponsor of the PERMIT Act and VORTEX Act and backer of the Aviation Workforce Development Act; cosponsored the SAVE America Act; chairs the T&I Water Resources and Environment subcommittee (2025–26) and previously chaired the Science Committee's Research and Technology subcommittee (2023–24).

people.name: Keisha Lance Bottoms
people.background: Former mayor of Atlanta (January 2018–January 2022), the city's 60th, who led the city through COVID-19 and the 2020 protests and did not seek a second term; Atlanta City Council member for District 11 (2010–2017). Served as senior advisor to President Biden for public engagement (June 2022–February 2023). Grew up in Atlanta; bachelor's from Florida A&M and J.D. from Georgia State University. Earlier an attorney and magistrate judge and executive director of the Atlanta and Fulton County Recreation Authority. Won the May 19, 2026 Democratic primary outright with 56.2% over Jason Esteves, Michael Thurmond, Geoff Duncan and three others.
people.ideology: Mainstream national Democrat and Biden White House alumna running on affordability, Medicaid expansion and voting rights; endorsed by Sens. Ossoff and Warnock, Joe Biden, EMILY's List, NEA, AFGE and Sierra Club Georgia.

positions.stance: Calls full Medicaid expansion a 'day-one priority' to cover about 300,000 uninsured Georgians, replacing the Georgia Pathways work-requirement program; also proposes revoking state licenses of insurers that repeatedly deny coverage and telling patients when AI is used in claim reviews (Oct. 6, 2026 debate). Proposes expanding prenatal and postpartum care in communities with limited access to maternal health services.

Would repeal Georgia's six-week abortion law and restore the pre-Dobbs Roe standard; ties the law to Georgia's maternal-mortality rates and proposes expanding prenatal and postpartum care and the pipeline of OB-GYNs, midwives and doulas.

Proposes property-tax relief and a homeowners-insurance tax credit, eliminating the 2.25% state tax on auto-insurance premiums, lowering the gas tax to 28 cents a gallon, eliminating state income tax for teachers, and letting local governments suspend or eliminate local sales taxes on groceries and other essentials.

Would guarantee universal pre-K for 4-year-olds, make kindergarten mandatory, revisit Georgia's decades-old school funding formula, back literacy programs and universal child care, and make community and technical colleges tuition-free; supports letting voters decide on casino gambling with some revenue for early learning.
Would raise Georgia's minimum wage to $15 an hour (roughly double the current $7.25).

Proposes a state 'John Lewis Voting Rights Act' expanding voting days and hours, accepting verified student IDs, making Election Day a state holiday, eliminating the State Election Board and adding poll-worker protections; said she is 'deeply concerned' about Trump's rhetoric on Fulton County elections.

positions.topic: Energy and utility bills / data centers
positions.stance: Calls for an immediate statewide pause on new data-center construction while the state assesses impacts ('There are too many unknowns'), with eminent domain limited to extreme cases; at the Oct. 6 debate she disputed Jackson's claim that she pushed a data-center project at Georgia Tech, saying it was part of a research hub.

Would increase state support for law enforcement and investigations plus violence-prevention, diversion and re-entry programs; points to police pay raises and the public-safety training center as mayor; is 'not opposed' to a moratorium on new Flock license-plate cameras over privacy and wants 'severe' penalties for misuse.

Would increase affordable-housing supply, speed permitting, expand renter and down-payment assistance, create a statewide affordable-housing trust fund and crack down on corporate landlords buying up homes.
Says cooperation with immigration authorities should be 'responsible and lawful'; as mayor she stopped allowing ICE to use Atlanta's city jail.

Says she 'will stand up to Donald Trump when necessary,' opposes his tariffs and attacks Jackson's pledge to be Trump's 'favorite governor'; campaigned jointly with Sen. Ossoff from May 2026 on a message of unity against the administration.
Would create a state Office of Small Business and expand business loans and grants; for farmers, proposes training and cooperative models.

people.name: Rick Jackson
people.background: Founder and CEO of Jackson Healthcare, an Alpharetta-based health-care staffing company reporting more than $3 billion in annual revenue; 72 years old and a political newcomer who has never held elected office. Grew up in Atlanta's Techwood Homes, lived in five foster homes and attended 13 schools; left David Lipscomb College because he could not afford to continue and in 1976 bought the staffing company where he worked. A philanthropist who led the effort to pass the Fostering Success Act, which lets foster youth attend Georgia public colleges tuition-free. Entered the race after Trump had endorsed Lt. Gov. Burt Jones (August 2025), finished second (32.5%) to Jones in the May 19 GOP primary, then won the June 16 runoff 52.6%–47.4%; he has spent nearly $200 million of his own money, among the largest self-funding efforts in U.S. history.
people.ideology: Self-described 'conservative outsider' running as a Trump-aligned businessman ('be like Trump, but with Southern tone') who also models himself on Gov. Kemp; endorsed by Trump (July 2026, after Trump's first pick Burt Jones lost), Kemp, Ted Cruz, Newt Gingrich and former Govs. Deal and Perdue; beat the Trump-endorsed Jones in the runoff.

positions.stance: Pledges to freeze increases in home valuations that drive property-tax bills, cut the state income tax in half within four years (promising not to seek a second term otherwise) and work toward eliminating it within eight, end state income tax on tips, freeze tuition, room and board at public colleges and technical schools, and use AI and audits to cut waste.

His Medicaid position has been reported differently over the campaign: in August 2026 the AJC reported he favored work requirements and a fixed federal block grant over full expansion; his 'Jackson Action Plan' (Sept. 2026) promised to 'close the coverage gap with intelligent Medicaid expansion' through a custom state-designed waiver with strict work, education or training requirements; at the Oct. 6 debate he said he supports expanding Medicaid if it does not jeopardize $4.5 billion in existing federal funding; and the AP (Oct. 2026) described his plan as expanding coverage through partnerships with private insurers without a traditional ACA Medicaid expansion. Also proposes state-level drug-price negotiation, strict price transparency, portable patient-controlled digital health records, 500 new inpatient psychiatric beds and more rural residency slots.

His campaign says he supports Georgia's six-week law as it stands, including exceptions for rape, incest and the mother's life; a recording from a Walton County campaign stop, reported earlier in the campaign, showed him sympathizing with a voter who questioned the rape exception and appearing open to additional limits, after which he reiterated support for the law as written.

Supports closer cooperation with the Trump administration on immigration enforcement and pledges to make Georgia 'first in the nation for deporting criminal illegal immigrants' (campaign site), which the AP describes as a promise to make Georgia a national leader in deportations; a primary ad using the phrase 'deported or departed' drew backlash, and he later said his focus was on 'people committing crimes and enforcing the law.'

Wants higher teacher pay (no amount specified as of Oct. 2026), improved childhood literacy, expanded career pathways, a stronger Parents' Bill of Rights, and a ban on DEI programs in state government, public universities and classrooms; endorsed Georgia's participation in the federal tax-credit scholarship program for private-school donations; backs barring boys from girls' sports, bathrooms and locker rooms.

Would leave Georgia's current election laws as they are, saying Kemp has gotten election-law changes right and 'Our last two elections have been good'; calls the system 'easy to vote and hard to cheat'; on federal/DOJ intervention said 'I don't think it's necessary unless Gov. Kemp thinks it's necessary,' and denied calling for National Guard deployment.

Backs more resources and personnel for sheriffs and tougher enforcement against violent crime, opposes what he calls 'soft-on-crime' policies, and said at the Oct. 6 debate, 'I will never ever abandon you by pulling out police when you need the protection the most'; opposes a moratorium on new Flock license-plate cameras while backing strict rules against misuse; his campaign announced endorsements from 104 Georgia sheriffs in August 2026.

Would require work or job training for 'able-bodied' adults receiving public assistance.
Has not proposed raising the minimum wage; emphasizes job training leading to $25-an-hour work instead ('Hopefully, you're not the one that is getting the $7.50 an hour').

Has at times promised to 'be like Trump, but with Southern tone'; said in July 2026 in Marietta he hoped to 'be this guy's favorite governor'; appeared at Trump's rallies in Dalton (Oct. 16) and Perry (Oct. 24, 2026), though he did not mention Trump in his Dalton speech; in the Oct. 6 debate he never named Trump, saying 'I will stand up to anybody, just like Brian Kemp has done.'
Would speed permanency decisions for children in foster care and expand mental-health access; cites the Fostering Success Act providing tuition-free public college for foster youth.

people.name: Josh McLaurin
people.background: Democratic state senator for District 14 (north Fulton County) since January 2023, after four years in the Georgia House (District 51, 2019–2023); did not run for re-election to the Senate in 2026. Attorney in Sandy Springs practicing business litigation and aviation law (formerly acting general counsel at ExpressJet Airlines, associate at Krevolin & Horst and Eleventh Circuit law clerk). people.ideology: Progressive-leaning Democrat who describes himself as a 'principled, committed fighter who can effectively promote progressive values' and says an ideal presiding officer can 'balance accountability with kindness and relationship building'; a frequent Trump critic known for jokes and satirical newscaster impressions; endorsed by Georgia AFL-CIO, Georgia Equality, Georgia Association of Educators, Sierra Club Georgia, Stacey Abrams and both U.S. senators.

Calls for limits on corporate ownership of single-family homes and zoning reform to allow smaller lots, townhouses and accessory dwelling units to increase supply and affordability.

Lists defending civil and voting rights as a top priority; says a U.S. Supreme Court ruling 'green-lit Republican attacks on Black voting power and democracy' and that the June 17, 2026 special session on redistricting 'threatens to erase Black voting power'; pledged to fight in that session ('I'm the only candidate in this race that will be there to fight').

Launched his campaign (May 2025) saying 'the Trump administration is tanking the economy and ignoring court orders'; opposes Trump's tariffs as needless and accuses Georgia Republicans of rubber-stamping Trump; publicized a 2016 text from JD Vance expressing concern about Trump.
Supports protecting workers' right to organize and says he would address rising costs by investing more in working families; endorsed by the Georgia AFL-CIO.

people.name: Greg Dolezal
people.background: Republican state senator for District 27 (Forsyth County) since January 2019; did not seek re-election in 2026, citing a self-imposed term limit. Born in Joliet, Illinois; bachelor's in business and communication from North Park University (2001). A Cumming businessman and co-owner of the software company Renewed Vision; formerly tour manager for musician Chris Tomlin and creative director at North Point Community Church's 7:22 ministry; founding member of Passion City Church. Chairs the Senate Transportation Committee, is vice chair of Appropriations and chaired the Special Committee on the Protection of Women's Sports. Finished second (23.1%) to John F. Kennedy in the May 19, 2026 primary, then won the June 16 runoff 54.2%–45.8%.
people.ideology: Trump-aligned conservative ('I stood with President Trump when it mattered most') who joined the post-2020 push for a special session to overturn Georgia's presidential result; cites Faith & Freedom Coalition, Turning Point Action and Americans for Prosperity scores; endorsed by Trump and, in the general election, by Gov. Kemp, who cited their work on income tax cuts, school vouchers and transportation funding.

positions.stance: Wants to eliminate property taxes, lower the income tax and cut special-interest tax breaks; says 'I've never voted for a tax increase'; Fox 5 described his runoff campaign as framed around 'strict fiscal conservatism' (May 2026).

Senate sponsor of SB 233, the Georgia Promise Scholarship Act (passed 2024), which provides $6,500 per student each school year for qualified education expenses (the AJC reports the scholarships have mainly benefited private-school students); supports expanding school choice and pledged to 'stop transgender indoctrination' in schools.

Sponsored SB 1, the Riley Gaines Act of 2025 (signed April 28, 2025), requiring school and college sports teams to be designated by biological sex and restricting restroom and overnight accommodations accordingly.

After the 2020 election joined three other GOP state senators in unsuccessfully seeking a special session to consider replacing Georgia's Democratic presidential electors; his campaign says he was 'personally thanked by President Trump for his work on election integrity'; supports changes to Georgia's voting systems (specifics not given).

Supports stricter immigration enforcement; ran AI-generated ads depicting Muslims attacking white Georgians that ended with 'Keep Georgia sharia free,' refused to apologize after criticism, and said Islam becoming part of America's governing philosophy is 'absolutely not' acceptable (June 2026).

Introduced a bill limiting large institutional investors' ownership of single-family homes and barring international private investors from buying rental property (passed the Senate, no House vote); proposes cutting building and permitting regulation and expanding financing options for first-time buyers.

Vowed to remove prosecutors he calls 'soft on crime'; is vice chair of the Senate special committee investigating Fulton County DA Fani Willis.

It's time we act like it.'

positions.stance: Favors keeping voting machines that generate a paper record, saying hand-marked ballots are less accurate; says 'We always act like there's a false choice' between machines and paper and 'I'm open to all of that' (Oct. 2026).
Says 'the federal government has no business overseeing elections,' amid the Trump administration's Fulton County investigation and lawsuit seeking Georgia voters' personal data.

Lists 'Protecting Voting Rights & Restoring Public Trust in Elections' and 'Transparency, Technology & Trust' as top priorities, including improving cybersecurity.
Would reduce barriers to forming small businesses and modernize professional licensing, 'cutting bureaucracy.'
Would use the office to safeguard seniors and vulnerable Georgians from fraud and scams.
Pledged to support farmers (Sept. 2025, per AP).

Attacks Fleming over the 2015 data breach exposing about 6 million voters' information while he was deputy secretary of state, saying 'just because you have a record of occupying a space doesn't mean you have a record of accomplishment.'
Believes the law should serve people, not power and has spent her life defending civil rights, expanding access, and standing against any effort to silence the voices of the people.

people.name: Tim Fleming
people.background: Republican state representative for House District 114 since January 2023; did not seek re-election in 2026. Small-business owner from Covington; attended the University of Georgia (political science). Longtime Brian Kemp aide: managed Kemp's 2010 secretary of state campaign, was named deputy secretary of state in 2013, managed Kemp's 2018 gubernatorial campaign and served as the governor's chief of staff (2019–Nov. 2020). Newton County commissioner (District 5) 2009–2013, elected at 25. Chaired the House Blue Ribbon Study Committee on Election Reforms and, per the AJC, chairs a House committee that proposes election-law changes; sits on Governmental Affairs. Led the May 19, 2026 GOP primary with 39.2% over Vernon Jones, Kelvin King and Gabriel Sterling, and won the June 16 runoff over Jones 64.5%–35.5%.
people.ideology: Longtime Kemp aide and establishment Republican who stresses loyalty to Trump ('I've always been there for Donald Trump') and election security; endorsed by Trump, Agriculture Commissioner Tyler Harper, U.S. Reps. Rick Allen, Andrew Clyde and Austin Scott and Frontline Policy Action; says there were 'serious irregularities' in 2020 but has not repeated Trump's claims of widespread fraud.

positions.stance: Wants Georgia to move from touchscreen ballot-marking devices to hand-marked paper ballots counted by scanners ('Over 70% of the country already votes this way'), with a new statewide system in place for 2028; the AJC (Oct. 2026) described his plan as hand-marked paper ballots printed on demand for voters who request them.
Says the law requiring removal of QR codes from ballots by July 1, 2026 'must be followed' and that he 'championed and voted for' it; opposed SB 214 because it would have extended that deadline.

Says 'There were serious irregularities in the 2020 election' and that 'Investigations have clearly documented issues and fraud in Fulton County,' but has stopped short of repeating Trump's claims of widespread fraud and says he is focused on the future.

Sponsored HB 397 (2025) to withdraw Georgia from the Electronic Registration Information Center (ERIC), with a July 1, 2027 transition date, ban absentee ballot drop-off the weekend before Election Day, and expand the State Election Board's rulemaking authority and role in voter-list accuracy; House leaders let it die without a final vote on the 2025 session's last night.

Cites 'defending voter ID laws' and 'keeping non-citizens off the rolls' as part of his record; pledges to deport immigrants in the country illegally who try to vote and to 'make it impossible for the Left to cheat in our elections.'
Says 'It's clear in the Constitution that elections are left to each state to run,' amid Trump administration moves on Fulton County and voter data.

Calls the 2021 Election Integrity Act (SB 202) 'a good step forward' but says 'there is a lot more work to do'; promised 'a more thoughtful, meaningful piece of elections legislation' for 2026 after HB 397 failed.
Priorities include faster professional licensing, cutting red tape for small businesses and better customer service.
Said in a June 2026 debate 'I've always been there for Donald Trump'; spoke at Trump's July 22, 2026 Marietta rally and holds Trump's endorsement.

people.name: Tanya Miller
people.background: Democratic state representative for House District 62 (Atlanta area) since January 2023 and chair of the House Democratic Caucus; did not seek re-election in 2026. Trial attorney and former prosecutor: assistant U.S. attorney in New York and a Fulton County assistant district attorney handling homicides and crimes against women and children; her private practice covers wrongful death, personal injury, criminal defense and civil rights. J.D. from Case Western Reserve University; raised in a working-class family. Serves on House Rules, Ethics, Code Revision and Information and Audits. Won the May 19, 2026 Democratic primary with 84.6% over Bob Trammell.
people.ideology: Democrat and House caucus leader who argued in the primary that Democratic voters 'want someone who will stand up to Donald Trump' and pledges to hold 'slumlords, price gougers, and greedy corporations accountable'; endorsed by EMILY's List, Georgia Equality, Georgia WIN List, Higher Heights, Sierra Club Georgia and AFSCME Local 1644, and backed by more than $2 million in Democratic Attorneys General Association spending.

positions.stance: Said in the primary she would take on Trump administration policies affecting tariffs, food aid, education funding and immigration enforcement when a case helps Georgians and the law supports it ('Does it help Georgians? Does the law support it?'); in October 2026 said partisanship would play no role and she would weigh litigation case by case.
Has questioned the constitutionality of Georgia's six-week abortion law, which is under challenge in state court (Apr. 2026).

Would target violent criminal networks, human trafficking, illegal guns and drugs such as fentanyl, crimes against children and domestic violence and support local police, while diverting nonviolent first-time offenders, backing re-entry and promoting 'evidence-based policies that reduce recidivism.'

Would investigate price gouging, challenge utility rate increases, create a unit to help small businesses and return money to consumers; says she introduced HB 1521 (to prevent Ponzi schemes), HB 1520 (to stop rent price-fixing by corporate landlords) and HB 733 (to 'level the playing field between insurance companies and consumers').

Supported a suit by 12 Democratic attorneys general to block Paramount Skydance's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, saying in July 2026 that they 'did what Georgia's attorney general refused to do: fight back' (the suit settled in September); pledged at her 2025 launch to hold 'slumlords, price gougers, and greedy corporations accountable.'
Opposes Gov. Kemp's 2025 limits on civil litigation (SB 68/SB 69 tort overhaul).
Opposes legislation letting voters approve new sales taxes to fund property-tax relief.
Lists safeguarding voting rights and ensuring fair elections as priorities; CBS News Atlanta reported in March 2026 that she pointed to growing anxiety over voting access and trust in elections.
Walked out of the House in 2025 to protest a bill barring public funding of gender-transition surgeries for prison inmates, an action Strickland calls partisan grandstanding.

Says she will ensure state's legal work is carried out with integrity, professionalism and transparency; says law should serve people, not political interests; says competence and quality—not backroom deals—should move state forward.
q: She will make sure the state’s legal work is carried out with integrity, professionalism, and transparency, protecting taxpayers while ensuring that Georgia’s government is accountable and acts in the public’s best interest.
Her career has been defined by one core principle: the law should serve people, not political interests.

positions.stance: Said she took direct action to break down systemic barriers for minority, women and veteran-owned businesses, will expand [something] to protect every family and business in Georgia, will crack down on consumer fraud, will take on corporate negligence and monopolistic practices and stressed need to oppose Republican policies.

As Attorney General, she will expand it to protect every family and business in Georgia.

positions.stance: Believes firsthand experience with human impact of public policy solidified commitment to fight for vulnerable communities; says she is a staunch advocate for abortion rights and will not take action supporting Georgia's abortion restriction law; pushed back against Republican-led policies and advocated for expanded healthcare access.
q: This firsthand experience with the human impact of public policy solidified her commitment to fighting for vulnerable communities.
She’s also a staunch advocate for abortion rights who’s vowed not to take any action in support of Georgia’s abortion restriction law, which she believes is unconstitutional.

positions.stance: Says Attorney General works with local police and sheriffs to keep communities safe by fighting criminal operations, understands importance of partnering with law enforcement to fight violent crime threatening families, and says Attorney General's job is to represent state, protect consumers, ensure public safety and uphold law.
q: The Attorney General works with local police and sheriffs to keep our communities safe by leading the fight against the most dangerous and complex criminal operations.
She understands the importance of partnering with and supporting local law enforcement, and she is prepared on day one to lead the fight against the violent crime that threatens our families.

positions.stance: Says she wants to use the office to improve affordability and push back against Trump's policies, wants to help lower housing costs by going after companies that use AI to boost rent prices and introduced legislation to bar companies from using AI to fix rent prices.
q: But candidate Tanya Miller said she wants to use the office to improve affordability and push back against President Donald Trump’s policies.
Miller also wants to help lower housing costs by going after companies like RealPage that use artificial intelligence software to boost rent prices.

Chairs the Senate Judiciary Committee and sits on Appropriations, Banking and Financial Institutions, Children and Families, Ethics, Health and Human Services and Public Safety; has served as a floor leader for Govs. Nathan Deal and Brian Kemp. Henry County High School (2002), B.B.A. in economics from Valdosta State (2006), J.D. from Florida Coastal School of Law (2009); practices law in McDonough. Won the May 19, 2026 GOP primary over Sen. Bill Cowsert, 71.6%–28.4%.

Kemp, with $1 million committed by the Republican Attorneys General Association; appeared at a Trump rally in Dalton (Oct. 2026).

positions.stance: Would expand gang and drug task forces to coordinate statewide crackdowns on violent crime, working with local, state and federal agencies against gangs, human trafficking and illegal drugs, and would protect seniors from scams; says 'We need to lock up people who need to be locked up' but 'we're also going to work to help people who need to get out of the system,' citing mental-health care in prisons as part of Deal-era criminal justice reform (2025).

Pledges to fight illegal immigration; in the primary said 'Georgia is still feeling the impact of four years of the Joe Biden open border' and that the next AG should support the president on border security.

Helped move Georgia's six-week abortion law through the legislature and says he will defend Republican-passed laws against court challenges ('They're trying to win at the courthouse what they couldn't win at the ballot box').
Supports gun owners' rights and helped pass Georgia's law allowing permitless carry.
Supports a 'parents' bill of rights' to 'protect our children from radical agendas in the classroom.'
Says the office should focus more on fighting crime, including election fraud, and lists defending 'election integrity' as a priority.

Backed the sweeping 2022 mental-health parity law requiring insurers to cover mental-health treatment on par with physical illness; lists expanding mental-health access, aiding foster children and protecting nursing-home residents among his priorities.

As Judiciary chair he presided over committee passage of Gov. Kemp's 2025 lawsuit-overhaul bills SB 68 and SB 69 (SB 68 passed 8–3 on party lines and SB 69 10–1 in February 2025); he has served as a floor leader for Kemp.

Says he will judge lawsuits case by case and that 'My metric moving forward will be what is best for Georgia families,' not what is best for either party; at his June 2025 campaign launch pledged to uphold conservative values against 'attacks from the Left.'
Emphasizes protecting seniors and small businesses from scams, identity theft and fraud, and says the AG should 'apply the law based on facts' without regard to party, wealth or connections.

Says children in state care were sleeping in government offices and hotel rooms with no bed, no school, and no one to count on, stands up for foster youth and vulnerable children, advances accountability standards for state programs, enforces Georgia’s laws firmly and impartially, and prioritizes protecting those in need through the law.

people.background: Gwinnett County Democrat and founder of Baby Katie's Pharm & Kitchen, a Snellville nonprofit that connects farmers with markets and families with fresh, locally grown food; also works with growers through Ag Explained and Pharm School and reports more than a decade working in infrastructure systems. Won the May 19, 2026 Democratic primary for Agriculture Commissioner over Sedrick Rowe Jr., 62.1%–37.9%, to challenge incumbent Tyler Harper.
people.ideology: Democrat running a consumer-protection and small-farm platform focused on food-safety inspections, market access and sustainability; endorsed by the Sierra Club Georgia Chapter; few other ideological markers documented.

positions.stance: Said at the Oct. 15, 2026 debate that food-safety inspections had fallen, citing 'a 45% drop in inspections in 2025,' and argued international World Cup visitors lacked confidence in local food; calls food-safety inspections a critical function of the office and wants licensing applied fairly and consistently statewide.
Criticized the state's handling of a Cyclospora contamination and called for faster, more transparent public-health notices.

Proposes mandatory agricultural resource impact reviews assessing water needs and drought effects before industrial projects are approved, and a formal voice for local growers when large projects could affect farm wells.
Says Georgia has neglected federal funding opportunities for a decade and should pursue federal grants to upgrade agricultural processing facilities.

Calls for regional food hubs at roughly $2 million each plus micro-hubs costing $150,000–$275,000; says Georgia Grown, which already exists in the Department of Agriculture, should work as a marketing and economic-development system providing stronger market access and connecting producers to consumers.

Prioritizes resources, education and market access for small and mid-sized growers, addressing rising costs for Georgia farmers and rural economic development; her campaign lists a 'Family Farm Plan' and a nine-pillar, four-to-eight-year governing agenda.

Emphasizes fuel-pump accuracy and food-safety inspections and wants licensing applied fairly and consistently statewide; the AJC lists consumer protection at the gas pump and elsewhere among her priorities.
Supports responsible agricultural practices, land protection, sustainable forestry and long-term sustainability.
Lists disaster response, fair markets and stronger rural communities among her campaign's focus areas.

Responding to Gov. Kemp's August 2026 endorsement of Harper, her campaign said the two share 'many of the same policies, policies that I believe have hurt Georgians,' which she said 'made our economy more unstable for working families, farmers, and small businesses.'

people.name: Tyler Harper
people.background: Incumbent Georgia Commissioner of Agriculture (the state's 17th), elected in 2022 and in office since January 9, 2023. Seventh-generation farmer and small-business owner from Ocilla (Irwin County); associate's degree from Abraham Baldwin Agricultural College and bachelor's in agricultural engineering from the University of Georgia. Served in the Georgia Senate (District 7, South Georgia) 2013–2023, chairing Natural Resources and the Environment (2021–22) and earlier Public Safety (2015 and 2017 sessions). Unopposed in the May 19, 2026 Republican primary (820,825 votes).
people.ideology: Mainstream agribusiness conservative whose campaign says it is 'Fighting to protect Georgia Farmers, Georgia Families, and Georgia's Food Supply'; endorsed by Gov. Brian Kemp; joined 11 other state agriculture commissioners in a 2024 letter opposing major banks' net-zero commitments; endorsed Trump-backed Tim Fleming for secretary of state.

positions.stance: Called the challenger's criticism of department staff 'a complete mischaracterization of the work that our people do at the department,' saying inspections increased even as regulated businesses grew 30% with 12% more staff, and called her attacks on employees 'disqualifying for her to hold this office' (Oct. 15, 2026 debate).
Says data centers should pay 100% of their utility and infrastructure costs, not use eminent domain, and lose state tax breaks, and that local communities should be able to reject unwanted projects.

Cites projections that Georgia will lose 800,000 acres of farmland by 2040; points to the Georgia Farmland Conservation Fund and restrictions on foreign adversaries buying agricultural land, both enacted during his tenure.

Says he has challenged corporate food mergers, expanded the Georgia Grown program into school cafeterias and used the Cooperative Interstate Shipment program to open interstate markets for Georgia beef; campaigns on lowering grocery and other costs for 'all 11 million Georgians.'

Cited a 550% surge in Mexican produce imports that he says hurts domestic growers, while urging federal leaders to protect Georgia poultry, pecan and cotton exporters from retaliatory tariffs; pledges to work to eliminate 'unfair trade deals.'
Signed off on new regulatory frameworks for consumable hemp products during his first term.
Pledges federal disaster aid for farmers that is 'delivered quickly'; his campaign site shows him visiting a pecan farm after Hurricane Helene (2024).
Priorities include new funding for farms and agribusiness, fighting 'burdensome regulations,' supporting agricultural education and expanding rural broadband.
Endorsed Trump-backed state Rep. Tim Fleming in the 2026 GOP secretary of state runoff.

Says Tyler has fought to lower cost of gas and groceries while protecting Georgia farmers, food supply, and families, earning bipartisan support; says Georgia farmers cannot afford unqualified commissioner leading Department of Agriculture, contrast between proven record vs. empty promises; believes best way to address food affordability is to strengthen domestic agriculture.
q: “Tyler has fought tirelessly to lower the cost of gas and groceries while protecting Georgia farmers, Georgia’s food supply, and Georgia families, and that’s why leaders from both parties are supporting his campaign.
Georgia farmers cannot afford to have an unqualified commissioner leading the Department of Agriculture, and the contrast in this race could not be more clear: a proven record vs. empty promises.”

positions.stance: Highlights ability to work across the aisle and bipartisan support from leaders of both parties, and highlighted bipartisan support from state leaders on both sides of the aisle.
q: Harper also highlighted his ability to work across the aisle to deliver for Georgians, and the bipartisan support from leaders of both parties his campaign has earned.

people.name: Keisha Sean Waites
people.background: Democratic nominee for Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner. Served three terms in the Georgia House (District 60, south metro Atlanta, 2012-2017) and as an at-large Atlanta City Council member (Post 3, January 2022-March 2024), resigning to run for Fulton County Clerk of Superior Court. Worked in FEMA's legislative and external affairs division; her campaign cites 15 years of federal service with the Department of Homeland Security and the Small Business Administration, including helping families and businesses recover from disasters. Born in Atlanta; attended Georgia Southern University, Atlanta Metropolitan State College and Georgia Perimeter College. A frequent candidate: Fulton County Commission chair (2017, 2018), U.S. House (2020) and the 2025 PSC District 3 special election (lost the Democratic runoff to Peter Hubbard). Led the May 19, 2026 Democratic primary (42.0%) and won the June 16 runoff over insurance agent DeAndre Mathis (about 59%).
people.ideology: Mainstream Democrat with a consumer-protection and affordability focus; says she will work with Republican legislators and operate within the 2025 tort-reform law; endorsed by Georgia Equality;

positions.topic: Insurance rating factors (ZIP code, credit score)
positions.stance: Wants to outlaw premiums based on ZIP code and credit score; at the Oct. 13, 2026 Atlanta Press Club debate said ensuring 'credit scores and ZIP codes are not a factor' in rates would be a priority 'on day one.'

Campaigns on challenging rate hikes by home and auto insurers and 'delivering real relief to Georgia families facing skyrocketing insurance premiums'; describes the office's job as fair regulation and rate review.

Proposes a Consumer Protection Unit inside the office to work with customers whose claims are denied, and investigations of denied claims; says 'Georgia consumers have no chance against a trillion dollar industry' (Oct. 2026).
Proposes a 'consumer fraud strike force' / dedicated task force to investigate scams targeting seniors and other vulnerable residents (2026).
Said in June 2026 that the next commissioner should operate within Gov. Kemp's 2025 law limiting jury awards rather than seek to undo it.
At the Oct. 2026 debate said many Georgians still face unequal access to health care and property insurance, blaming federal cuts and the failure to extend ACA premium subsidies.
Criticized the office's response after Hurricane Helene, saying Georgians lost the chance to appeal insurance denials; said she would 'restore this office to its original intent' (Oct. 2026).
Called for a thorough investigation and inspection of all rides before Six Flags Over Georgia reopened, pledging 'this will never happen again in the state of Georgia' (Oct. 2026).
Says she will work with Republican lawmakers to address discriminatory insurance practices: 'I don't care if you're a Republican or Democrat' (June 2026).
Addresses bullying with comprehensive legislation and supports cost free tuition for children of public safety officials disabled or killed in the line of duty.
q: She authored and sponsored HB 40 comprehensive legislation addressing bullying in which her efforts received the support and endorsement of the nationally renowned law firm Montlick and Associates and a plethora of national Anti-Bullying organizations.
Keisha authored and sponsored HB 54, (the Fallen Hero Bill) to support families by providing cost free tuition to the children of public safety officials disabled or killed in the line of duty.

people.record: In the Georgia House she sponsored a bill creating voluntary donations through income-tax returns and driver's licenses to fund tuition for children of first responders killed or injured on duty. On the Atlanta City Council she backed a crackdown on reckless drivers, a stricter youth curfew and a citywide public-safety task force. Ethics: as of June 2026 she was appealing an Atlanta ethics ruling that she owes the city nearly $25,000 for taxpayer-funded newsletters used for campaign advantage plus $5,000 in fines, with a hearing set for September 2026.

signals.claim: Would likely seek legislation barring ZIP code and credit score as insurance rating factors.
signals.basis: Her stated plan to work with former General Assembly colleagues to 'ensure that credit scores and ZIP codes are not a factor in terms of assessing rates,' which she called a 'day one' priority (Oct. 2026 debate), and her campaign advocacy to outlaw ZIP code and credit score-based premiums.

signals.claim: May publicly advocate for extending federal health-insurance subsidies or for state measures to widen access to coverage.
signals.basis: Oct. 2026 debate remarks blaming federal cuts and the failure to extend subsidies for unequal access to health care.

signals.claim: May push for tighter state amusement-ride inspection requirements or staffing after the Six Flags fatality.
signals.basis: Her debate pledge that such a death 'will never happen again' and call for inspections of all rides.

people.name: John King
people.background: Republican incumbent Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner since July 2019, appointed by Gov. Brian Kemp in June 2019 after Commissioner Jim Beck was indicted and suspended; won a full term in 2022 (54.1% over Democrat Janice Laws Robinson). Born in Mexico, he is Georgia's first Hispanic statewide constitutional officer. A former Atlanta police officer and Doraville police chief, he served about four decades in the Army National Guard, retiring as a major general in 2023. Bachelor's degree from Brenau University and a graduate degree from the U.S. Army War College. Launched a 2026 U.S. Senate bid in May 2025 and withdrew in July 2025 to seek reelection; unopposed in the 2026 Republican primary.
people.ideology: Kemp-aligned Republican (appointed by Kemp in 2019; advocated for Kemp's 2025 tort-reform law) and self-described 'lawman and soldier'; the AJC describes him as a vocal Trump supporter; endorsed Rick Jackson over Lt. Gov. Burt Jones in the 2026 GOP gubernatorial primary; campaign platform includes lawsuit reform, the Georgia Access state exchange, recovering money from insurers and fraud enforcement.

positions.stance: Advocated for Gov. Kemp's 2025 tort-reform legislation and credits tort reform with lowering auto premiums; his campaign says he is now 'focused on making sure insurance companies follow through on their promise to lower rates.'

In Nov.-Dec. 2025 announced approved auto rate decreases from State Farm (about 3%), Safeco (about 5%) and Liberty Mutual (5.7%), crediting tort reform and anti-fraud work and saying 'I am confident that we will see rates further decline across Georgia.'

At the Oct. 13, 2026 debate said the 'whole authority had been taken away from the insurance department to intervene in rates' and that he will ask the Legislature to restore some of it: 'I'm not going to give up on that.'

Helped move Georgia from the federally operated marketplace to the state-run Georgia Access exchange; his campaign says insurers offering plans grew from four to ten and 1.3 million Georgians enrolled in its first year. Responding at the Oct. 2026 debate to criticism over federal cuts and unextended subsidies, said private health insurance 'has stepped up in its place' and 'the key there is to go and hold insurance companies accountable. And we've done that.'

Has focused on 'increasing fines and expanding legal pathways to take on bad-actor insurance companies'; his campaign says the office has imposed more than $22 million in fines since 2019, including a $5 million fine it calls the largest in Georgia history, and recovered more than $100 million for consumers, a figure he repeated at the Oct. 2026 debate.

Campaign says the office has arrested more than 500 arsonists since 2019, more than tripled arson K-9s and expanded fraud investigations; proposes expanded investigations into scams and warned at the Oct. 2026 debate about fake insurance products.
Campaign says the office deploys 'teams on the ground' and sets up 'claims villages to connect storm victims directly with providers' after storms.
Warned at the Oct. 2026 debate against letting artificial intelligence determine insurance policies.

Said his office inspected all rides before the season and is investigating the fatality; declined detail citing the open investigation: 'We're going to go with this where the facts take us' (Oct. 2026).
Described by the AJC as a 'vocal supporter of President Donald Trump.' Endorsed Rick Jackson for governor in April 2026, calling him 'our best shot at winning in November.'

people.record: Appointed commissioner in 2019 and elected in 2022. Oversaw the transition from the federal marketplace to the state-run Georgia Access exchange, supported the 2025 tort-reform law, and approved a series of auto-insurance rate decreases in late 2025. Campaign cites more than $100 million recovered for consumers, $22 million in fines, and 500-plus arson arrests since 2019 (self-reported figures).

signals.claim: Would likely ask the 2027 General Assembly for legislation restoring the commissioner's prior-approval or rate-intervention authority.
signals.basis: His Oct. 13, 2026 debate statement that he will ask the Legislature to restore rate authority and will not 'give up on that.'

signals.claim: Would likely support further lawsuit-reform measures if insurers' rate reductions stall.
signals.basis: 'Lawsuit Reform' is a campaign plank; he supported the 2025 law and ties premium relief to it.

signals.claim: May back regulation or legislation limiting insurers' use of AI in underwriting and claims decisions.
signals.basis: Oct. 2026 debate warning against letting AI determine insurance policies.

people.name: Lydia Powell
people.background: Democratic nominee for State School Superintendent. Assistant principal at Hampton High School in Henry County, with 26 years in education as a certified teacher including 11 in school leadership; taught social studies in DeKalb, Clayton, Fayette and Henry counties (and in Lee County, Florida), in alternative, high-achieving and low-income schools. Her campaign lists graduation from Florida A&M University, Florida State University and 'The University of Sarasota'; she uses the title 'Dr.' Chairs the Fayetteville Ethics Committee and is a former PTSO president. First run for public office; won the May 19, 2026 Democratic primary outright with 50.5% over Hancock County Superintendent Anton Anthony and 2018 nominee Otha Thornton, running strongly in rural counties.
people.ideology: Mainstream public-education Democrat; criticizes the SB 233 Promise Scholarship voucher program, saying it 'can potentially defund public schools'; campaigns on rural schools and on giving educators a seat at the table; endorsed by Georgia Equality.

positions.stance: Lists 'School Choice & Vouchers (SB 233)' among her key issues, saying the program 'can potentially defund public schools' (2025 survey); at the Oct. 2026 debate questioned spending more than $100 million on private-school vouchers while putting $70 million toward literacy coaches.
Says Georgia must modernize the Quality Basic Education formula and add a direct poverty weight, citing that more than 70% of students face economic hardship (Oct. 2026).

Supports evidence-based literacy instruction; says reading challenges cannot be dismissed and basic word recognition alone does not prepare students to analyze text; noted one statewide literacy coach serves all 159 districts (Oct. 2026).
Wants to expand connectivity and advanced coursework in rural Georgia; says rural communities 'don't see us enough, so I have to go there' (2026).
Said eighth-grade math scores declined this year, lower-performing schools lack funds for certified math teachers, and coaches often lack training while overseeing up to 15 teachers (Oct. 2026).
Criticized the delays surrounding the Advanced Placement African American Studies course under the incumbent (Oct. 2026).
Promises change including a seat at the table for educators: 'My No. 1 priority is that people's voices are heard' (2026).

signals.claim: Would likely use the office to oppose expansion of the Promise Scholarship voucher program and to publicize its cost relative to public-school needs.
signals.basis: Her stated opposition to SB 233 and her Oct. 2026 debate contrast of $100M+ in vouchers with $70M for literacy coaches.

signals.claim: Would likely lobby the General Assembly for a QBE overhaul adding a permanent poverty weight.
signals.basis: Oct. 2026 debate proposal for a direct poverty weight in the funding formula.

people.name: Richard Woods
people.background: Republican incumbent State School Superintendent since January 2015, seeking a fourth term. A former Irwin County social studies teacher (14 years) who also served as assistant principal, principal, curriculum director, testing coordinator, pre-K director and alternative-school director; more than 30 years in pre-K-12 education. Born in Pensacola, Florida; lives in Tifton; attended Kennesaw State University (undergraduate) and Valdosta State University (master's). Won the 2014 GOP runoff by 713 votes and general elections in 2014 (55.1%), 2018 (53.0%) and 2022 (54.2%). In 2026 he fell about 1,000 votes short of a primary majority (49.9%) and beat Candler County Superintendent Fred 'Bubba' Longgrear 51.5%-48.5% in the June 16 runoff, despite House Speaker Jon Burns, the House and Senate education chairs and Senate Majority Leader Jason Anavitarte backing Longgrear and roughly $900,000 in spending against Woods by Conservatives for Strong Schools.
people.ideology: Conservative Republican campaigning on what The Current calls a 'conservative agenda' (removing Common Core, shrinking the federal role in education, not allowing transgender girls to play girls' sports) but at odds with GOP legislative leadership over literacy policy and accessibility; frames his work as 'serving people over politicians' and giving teachers 'freedom in the classroom.' Frontline Policy Action backed 'Change' over him in the 2026 primary.

positions.stance: Asked at the Oct. 13, 2026 debate about tax dollars for private schools, said 'This is a legislative decision' and that his duty is 'making sure that we are fully funded in public education.'

Pushes back on calling the state's reading results a crisis, describing annual Georgia Milestones results as a 'single testing snapshot'; says federally funded literacy coaches produced a 29% gain at struggling schools (Oct. 2026). House lawmakers insisted on cutting Woods out of decision-making on the 2026 literacy law after years of friction, including a 2023 dispute over a literacy bill and a 2024 fight over screening tests.
Cites full removal of Common Core standards by 2023 and credits it with keeping student performance moving forward; touts return of phonics, cursive and financial literacy.

Supports downgrading if not dismantling the U.S. Department of Education: 'the federal government should not have anything to do with public education'; said Title I and special-education funds would not be affected by its closure (Sept. 2025).
Said 'LGBT is not a problem in our state, and I'm proud to say I have not allowed any boys to play girls' sports' (Sept. 2025).

positions.topic: AP African American Studies / divisive concepts
positions.stance: In 2024 declined to recommend adding AP African American Studies to the state catalog under the divisive-concepts law, drew bipartisan criticism and backed down; in Oct. 2026 said he created course numbers letting schools offer African American, Native American and women's studies.

Says he delivered on 'ending the massive amount of testing we were doing' and sought to make the state accountability system less based on test scores; lawmakers and advocates rejected the accountability change.
Said the state already added a poverty weight to the budget two years ago and that broader QBE changes must balance property-tax relief with steady school revenue (Oct. 2026).
Says pushing all students toward four-year universities was a mistake and vocational school should be a more viable option; cites growth in career-technical education and graduation rates.
Announced plans to shift federal funds from reading coaches to new math coaches (Oct. 2026).

Lawmakers said in 2026 they rarely heard from him; he responded that 'access has never been an issue' and that he met with the Speaker's and Lieutenant Governor's staff on literacy and will 'continue to work with our legislators.'

Supports expanding state salary scale beyond 21 years and additional pay for teachers; says state salary scale does not provide step increases for beginning and veteran teachers; would expand step raises across a teacher’s entire career to recruit and retain teachers.
q: He continues to fight for additional pay as well as extending the state salary scale beyond 21 years.

The state salary scale does not provide salary step increases for beginning teachers with 0-2 years of experience or veteran teachers with more than 21 years of experience, meaning teachers at both ends of their careers receive flat pay -- this must change!

positions.stance: Supports prioritizing student safety; supports increasing school resource officers and mental health resources; supports providing on-the-ground support for threat assessments and safety plans.
q: The safety of students must remain a top priority.

We must increase both School Resource Officers (SROs) and mental health resources; coordinate best practices and training; secure facilities; and collaborate with community organizations and public safety partners.

positions.stance: Supports evaluating and updating funding for all positions to reflect true costs.
q: School districts only earn $11,000 per bus driver in state funding; funding for all positions need to be evaluated and updated to reflect true costs.

people.record: Twelve years as superintendent: oversaw removal of Common Core standards (completed 2023) and the return of cursive and financial-literacy instruction, and touts improved graduation rates; in 2024 backed down from an attempt to halt AP African American Studies under the divisive-concepts law; repeatedly clashed with lawmakers over literacy legislation, culminating in House lawmakers cutting him out of decision-making on the 2026 literacy law. Educators First said in 2022 he had reduced high-stakes testing and championed teacher pay raises. He has never led a local school district.

signals.claim: Would likely continue to resist test-score-heavy accountability and seek to reduce the weight of Georgia Milestones.
signals.basis: His multi-year effort to make the accountability system less test-based and his 'single testing snapshot' framing at the Oct. 2026 debate.

signals.claim: Is unlikely to publicly oppose Promise Scholarship expansion and would likely defer to the legislature while asking for full public-school funding.
signals.basis: His Oct. 2026 debate answer calling vouchers 'a legislative decision.'

signals.claim: May support state measures to absorb or replace federal education functions if the U.S. Department of Education is dismantled.
signals.basis: Sept. 2025 statements supporting downgrading or dismantling the department and saying Title I and special-education funds would be unaffected by its closure.

signals.claim: May again act to restrict course content he views as covered by the divisive-concepts law.
signals.basis: The 2024 AP African American Studies dispute, though he reversed course under bipartisan criticism.

people.name: Nikki Porcher
people.background: Democratic nominee for Commissioner of Labor. U.S. Air Force veteran, former Georgia public-school teacher and founder (2016) of Buy From a Black Woman, an Atlanta-based nonprofit supporting Black women entrepreneurs that The Story Exchange says has helped over 700 business owners. her campaign describes her as a single mother who worked multiple jobs, and she has said, 'I am the Georgian who has been unemployed looking for work.' First run for office: finished first in the five-way May 19, 2026 Democratic primary (30.8%) and won the June 16 runoff over community organizer Michelle Sanchez with about 62%.
people.ideology: Labor-aligned Democrat: defends unions and her union endorsements ('I stand with Georgia workers'), supports raising Georgia's $5.15 state minimum wage and human oversight of AI hiring tools; endorsed by Georgia Equality. Her opponent says she 'stands with far-left agenda and labor bosses.'

positions.stance: Says the Department of Labor's computer processing technology has been outdated since the 1980s, that the new system's target slipped from fall 2026 to 2027, and that the digital portal fails frustrated applicants (Oct. 2026); in the runoff she emphasized awareness of existing programs: 'People can't take advantage of training opportunities if they don't know they exist.'

Supports unions, crediting them with 'safe workplaces, fair wages, and the actual support that workers need every day'; at the October 2026 debate said state law does not make union dues mandatory in unionized workplaces, that unions extend protections to non-paying workers, and 'I will fight to make sure that workers are first in this state.'
Wants to raise Georgia's state minimum wage from $5.15 an hour; notes increase proposals have repeatedly stalled in the General Assembly (2026).

Calls child care a top priority ('At the top is child care as a workforce issue') and 'economic infrastructure'; The Story Exchange, reporting on that priority, cites costs rising from $16,500 in 2020 to $20,600 and child-care deserts in about 32% of Georgia ZIP codes (2026).

Says rural counties lack career centers and training, with commutes of 75-80 minutes; would expand technical-college, apprenticeship and workforce partnerships and build hiring pipelines between career centers and local employers.
Wants state rules requiring human oversight when employers use algorithms to screen, hire or dismiss workers, and retraining so workers can use AI as an assistive tool (Oct. 2026).

Said 'I don't trust the numbers' about the state's 3.2% August 2026 unemployment rate, citing July figures showing Georgia losing jobs; wants better labor data so 'the numbers are reflecting what's truly happening' (2026).

Said at the Oct. 2026 debate that people in Georgia deserve protection regardless of origin and raised concerns about workers' fear of ICE activity; criticized her opponent's support for Rick Jackson over his deportation rhetoric.

Says Georgia ranks first for business but last on Oxfam America's list of the best and worst states for workers: 'we're number one in business because too many Georgians are working two jobs just to get by'; says 'When we invest in people, businesses, and fairness, Georgia's economy grows stronger for everyone.'
Would build partnerships helping small businesses hire, train and retain workers, drawing on her nonprofit work.

Would increase coordination between labor, workforce, and child care systems; believes government systems should work for people but many feel ignored or left behind; believes no one should feel abandoned by systems designed to help them move forward.
q: Increase coordination between labor, workforce, and child care systems across Georgia

Nikki believes government systems should work for the people they are meant to serve, but too many Georgians feel frustrated, ignored, or left behind when trying to access workforce services and support.

endorsements: Unnamed labor unions (per FOX 5 debate coverage, Oct. 2026)

signals.claim: Would likely use the office to oppose anti-union or expanded right-to-work legislation.
signals.basis: Her Oct. 2026 debate defense of unions and organizing and her union endorsements.

signals.claim: Would likely advocate publicly for a state minimum-wage increase and for rules requiring human oversight of algorithmic hiring, though neither is within the commissioner's own authority.
signals.basis: Her stated support for raising the $5.15 wage and for state rules requiring human oversight when employers use algorithms to screen, hire or dismiss workers.

signals.claim: May support child-care subsidies or employer child-care incentives administered through workforce programs.
signals.basis: Child care as her stated top priority and 'economic infrastructure.'

signals.claim: May resist cooperation with federal immigration enforcement in workplaces.
signals.basis: Oct. 2026 debate remarks on protecting workers regardless of origin and concern about ICE fear.

people.name: Bárbara Rivera Holmes
people.background: Republican incumbent Commissioner of Labor since April 2025, appointed by Gov. Brian Kemp on March 18, 2025 to succeed Bruce Thompson, who died in November 2024; the first Latina to hold a statewide constitutional office in Georgia. Born in San Juan, Puerto Rico, to a family that fled Cuba; degrees in journalism and Spanish from Florida Southern College. A former Albany Herald journalist, she led the Albany Area Chamber of Commerce as president and CEO from 2016 (she cites 20 years as a local chamber executive) and earlier worked in economic development in southwest Georgia; appointed to the University System of Georgia Board of Regents by Gov. Nathan Deal in 2018 and served on the Georgia Rural Development Council. Lives in Albany. Said at her March 2025 appointment that she would seek a full term in 2026, and was unopposed in the 2026 Republican primary.
people.ideology: Kemp-aligned, business/chamber-wing Republican: supports right-to-work laws and opposes mandatory union dues, promotes Kemp's 'Top State for Talent' workforce agenda, backs Rick Jackson for governor (per FOX 5 debate coverage) and says 'a nation without a secure border is not a nation at all.'

positions.stance: Says she launched the largest unemployment insurance modernization effort in state history; her campaign calls it 'the largest unemployment insurance modernization initiative in Georgia's history,' replacing the old system with a 'secure, cloud-based platform' to speed claims and reduce fraud (2025-26).

Supports Georgia's right-to-work laws and says mandatory union dues harm economic freedom; at the October 2026 debate asked Porcher, 'Do you support Georgia's right to work laws or do you stand with big labor bosses who want compulsory dues?' and said, 'My opponent stands with far-left agenda and labor bosses.'

Wants to expand employer partnerships in construction, automotive repair and advanced manufacturing, upskill current workers, and work with colleges and workforce boards under Kemp's 'Top State for Talent' effort.
Says nearly every modern job is becoming a technology job and the state should work with employers to move staff into higher-level roles (Oct. 2026).

Called the issue 'deeply personal' because her family fled communist Cuba and said, 'America is also a nation of laws, and a nation without a secure border is not a nation at all'; says she supports leaders who protect economic freedom and secure borders (Oct. 2026).

Cites 3.2% unemployment in August 2026, record labor-force participation, 25,000 new jobs and $35 billion in capital investment last fiscal year: 'Unemployment is down to the lowest point in two and a half years, and we continue to grow jobs.'

Said in Oct. 2025 that 'we have outdated regulations that make it just more difficult for people to do work with the Georgia Department of Labor' and that she wants to cut red tape, without specifying which rules; says she is working to restore the department's credibility.
Says the department is improving links between small employers and talent pipelines, simplifying hiring and expanding job-matching systems.
Supports Rick Jackson in the 2026 governor's race (per Oct. 2026 debate coverage).

Believes every Georgian deserves access to good-paying jobs, workforce training and a system that works for them, will overhaul outdated systems to deliver faster support, is committed to making the department a partner in job creation, says unemployed workers should access support quickly and with dignity and will advocate for policies that strengthen wages and improve worker protections.
q: She believes every Georgian deserves access to good-paying jobs, workforce training, and a system that works for them — not against them.
Bárbara will overhaul outdated systems, improve technology and streamline services to deliver faster, more reliable support for workers and businesses.

positions.stance: Will strengthen partnerships with colleges and universities, employers and training programs to open new pathways for Georgians.
q: Bárbara will strengthen partnerships with colleges and universities, employers and training programs to open new pathways for Georgians — whether in manufacturing, technology, health care or other in-demand industries.

people.record: Appointed commissioner in 2025 after a roughly three-month vetting process; launched a departmental strategic plan and an overhaul of the decades-old unemployment-claims technology. The department's FY2025 budget of about $8.5 million was nearly $10 million below what agency leaders requested, and Democrats said in 2025 they saw no signs of progress; her opponent says the modernization target slipped from fall 2026 to 2027.

signals.claim: Would likely support legislation reinforcing right-to-work protections or restricting union-dues collection.
signals.basis: Her Oct. 2026 debate statements supporting right-to-work laws and opposing mandatory union dues.

signals.claim: Is unlikely to support raising Georgia's state minimum wage above the federal floor.
signals.basis: Chamber-of-commerce background and a business-aligned workforce platform; her campaign says she backs 'policies that strengthen wages' but states no position on the minimum wage.

signals.claim: May support stronger employer verification or cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
signals.basis: Her 'secure border' remarks at the Oct. 2026 debate and support for Rick Jackson.

signals.claim: Would likely keep the department closely aligned with the governor's economic-development and talent initiatives.
signals.basis: Kemp appointment and her promotion of the 'Top State for Talent' agenda.
