people.name: Peter Hubbard
people.background: Democratic incumbent Public Service Commissioner for District 3 since January 1, 2026, after defeating Republican incumbent Fitz Johnson with about 63% in the November 4, 2025 special election for a one-year term; he and Alicia Johnson are the first Democrats on the PSC since 2006. A clean-energy advocate and energy-market analyst with about 15 years in the sector, including Pace Global (a Siemens business) and renewable and battery project development, he founded the nonprofit Georgia Center for Energy Solutions in 2019 and testified before the PSC. Bachelor's degrees in physics and mathematics from the University of Memphis and a master's from Johns Hopkins SAIS; served in the Peace Corps in Morocco. Born in Akron, Ohio; an Atlanta resident for about a decade. Lost the 2022 Democratic primary for House District 90; unopposed in the 2026 Democratic primary for a full six-year term.
people.ideology: Clean-energy Democrat who describes himself as practical about fossil fuels ('not simply anti fossil') and is not opposed to nuclear power; endorsed by Sen. Jon Ossoff, Stacey Abrams, the SPLC Action Fund, the Asian American Advocacy Fund and the Southern Alliance for Clean Energy Action Fund.

positions.stance: Says 'The average family is now paying $600 more per year for electricity' (2025 questionnaire); has demanded an independent audit of Georgia Power's profit margin, which his campaign calls 'significantly above national averages.'

Says 'A large data center pays 80% less than a residential customer pays for the same electricity' and that the PSC's new rule leaves what is fair largely to Georgia Power; promotes a cost analysis estimating that data-center electricity discounts shift more than $1 billion in infrastructure costs onto residential customers, and wants public input before Georgia Power signs contracts with customers using over 100 MW (2025-26).

On Feb. 18, 2026 voted with Alicia Johnson to reconsider the December 2025 certification of nearly 10,000 MW of new gas plants, battery storage and some solar (failed 3-2) and separately moved to deny certification of the McIntosh combustion turbine and other planned gas units, which the Republican majority voted down: 'I'm not satisfied that there are adequate consumer protections in place.'

Says 'the 2025 IRP was flawed and led to the approval of thousands of megawatts of new gas-fired capacity'; before testifying to the PSC in May 2025 he built a model of Georgia Power's system with a National Renewable Energy Laboratory tool and concluded growth could be met while lowering bills through clean energy; would re-examine the plan against a clean-energy portfolio with demand-side management.

Criticizes the roughly $35 billion Plant Vogtle expansion because ratepayers, not just shareholders, bore its costs, saying such costs should not have been 'borne by the rate payers'; cites Vogtle Units 3 and 4 as an example of risk shifted to customers (2025-26).

Wants solar to grow from about 7% of Georgia's energy to 30-50% before pursuing more expensive resources; supports community and warehouse-rooftop solar; says rooftop-solar customers 'only receive one-third of the value of the solar they sell back to the grid' and that a 5,000-customer monthly net-metering pilot promised in the 2019 IRP was never followed up (2025).
Says he is 'not simply anti fossil' and sees a small role for dispatchable gas, but argues its public-health and climate costs are not fully counted (2025).
Not opposed to nuclear power, which emits no carbon, though he criticizes how Plant Vogtle's costs fell on ratepayers (2025).
Says 'all cost effective energy efficient programs and policies should be implemented,' calling efficiency 'the lowest hanging fruit' (2025).
Criticizes that roughly $2 billion a year in coal and gas fuel costs are '100% passed-through to the customer with 0% risk worn by the utility' (2025).

Testified in front of the state legislature on the need for legislation to protect consumers, says the Commission may protect the public interest and fulfill its responsibilities, and states the proposed new rates go into effect 30 days from the filing date unless commissioners vote to suspend them.
q: -Testified in front of the state legislature on the need for legislation to protect consumers.
To protect the public interest and to fulfill its responsibilities, the Commission may:

positions.stance: Says power was cut in 95-degree heat one day after payment-arrangement date over $100 balance, consumer on breathing machine had service cut over past-due balance despite doctor's statement, and disconnection followed within a day of payment-arrangement date the consumer believed met.
q: Power cut in 95-degree heat one day after her payment-arrangement date, over a balance of roughly $100.
Consumer on a 24-hour breathing machine says service was cut over a past-due balance despite a submitted doctor's statement.

positions.stance: Supports conservative and thoughtful free-market approach without state-sponsored financial incentives.
q: He has accomplished this through a conservative and thoughtful free-market approach without putting upward pressure on rates and without state-sponsored financial incentives.

positions.stance: Voted to provide Georgians as much relief as possible.
q: “Summer is coming, so I voted to provide Georgians as much relief as possible,” Hubbard said.

people.record: In office since Jan. 1, 2026. On Feb. 18, 2026 voted to reconsider the PSC's December 2025 certification of Georgia Power's nearly 10,000 MW expansion (failed 3-2 on party lines) and moved to deny certification of the McIntosh combustion turbine and other gas units (voted down by the Republican majority). Has demanded an independent audit of Georgia Power's profit margin, promoted a data-center cost-shift analysis, proposed an amendment requiring an investigation of Georgia Power's costs and practices before certification of a new rate agreement, and testified to the legislature on consumer protection. Before office, testified to the PSC in May 2025 using his own model of Georgia Power's system.

people.name: Fitz Johnson
people.background: Republican nominee for PSC District 3 and the seat's former commissioner (Aug. 26, 2021-Dec. 31, 2025), appointed by Gov. Brian Kemp in July 2021 to replace Chuck Eaton; lost the November 2025 special election to Peter Hubbard 37%-63%. Won the May 19, 2026 Republican primary over Brandon Martin by about 3,000 votes (50.2%-49.8%) after an administrative law judge ruled in April 2026 that his legal domicile remained in Fulton County despite time spent at a Cobb County home. U.S. Army officer 1981-2002 (Medical Service Corps; 10 years active duty and 11 in the reserves, reaching the rank of major); business owner (ASID Group International, Eagle Group International), former owner of the Atlanta Beat women's professional soccer team and a Realtor. B.A. The Citadel (1985), M.Ed. Troy University (1991), J.D. University of Kentucky (1998). The second African American and first Black Republican to serve on the PSC. Lost the 2014 GOP primary for school superintendent and a 2020 Cobb County Commission race.
people.ideology: Kemp-appointed Republican running on an 'America First energy agenda': campaigns against the 'Green New Deal,' 'costly climate mandates' and 'out-of-state climate activists'; supports an 'all of the above' energy approach; endorsed by Veterans for America First.

positions.stance: Voted for all six Georgia Power rate increases since 2023 (per SACE) and for the three-year base-rate freeze approved in mid-2025; says he won't raise rates again if he returns (2026).

Voted for the 2025 PSC rule expanding oversight of Georgia Power's large-load contracts and says 'Georgia's large-load customer protections are among the strongest in the country'; says the commission has '100 percent, without doubt' protected customers from data-center costs and that 'We're getting a better grid, a stronger grid, paid for by large load customers' (2026).

In December 2025 voted to certify Georgia Power's nearly 10,000 MW expansion, which SACE describes as tens of billions of dollars in new power plants primarily to serve data centers; SACE says he voted for all of Georgia Power's proposed gas expansions over the past five years.
In December 2023 joined a unanimous vote approving recovery of about $7.6 billion in Vogtle cost overruns from customers; voted for the related roughly 6% rate increase.
Voted in July 2022 and in 2025 to extend the lives of several coal units previously slated for retirement.

Supports an 'all of the above' energy approach and says fossil fuels should remain part of Georgia's energy mix; in 2022, after PSC staff recommended 10%, proposed an amendment raising EV-charging funding to 65% of Georgia Power's $81 million request.

Says he has worked to stop the 'Green New Deal,' opposes 'costly climate mandates' and warns against handing Georgia's grid to 'out-of-state climate activists'; campaign site says he stopped Washington's climate agenda 'at the state line.'
As commissioner voted to increase Universal Service Fund disbursements to nonprofits funding bill assistance and appliance upgrades for low-income customers.
Platform planks include 'Keep Georgia the #1 State To Do Business' and 'Unleash American Energy Dominance' with an 'America First energy agenda.'

Did not attend the October 2025 Atlanta Press Club PSC debate, where Hubbard questioned an empty podium; said his record 'speaks for itself' and 'doesn't need a format that rewards sound bites and snark rather than serious discussion of complex kitchen table issues.'

people.record: PSC commissioner Aug. 2021-Dec. 2025. people.name: Shelia Edwards
people.background: Democratic nominee for the open PSC District 5 seat. A Cobb County community advocate, publicist and business owner with more than 35 years in corporate, government and communications roles: press secretary and district director for U.S. Rep. David Scott, communications chief for DeKalb County government and the Fulton County District Attorney's office, and interim executive director of the Georgia House Democratic Caucus (2024); earlier worked for Lockheed Space Operations at Kennedy Space Center on the shuttle program. B.A. in journalism from Benedict College (1984), Emory University executive education in managerial leadership (2002), and a current graduate student at Georgia State's Andrew Young School. Lost 2016 and 2018 Democratic primaries for House District 39 and ran for Cobb Commission chair in 2024; won the 2022 Democratic primary for PSC District 3 (54.7%) before that general election was canceled after a federal court ruling in litigation over how commissioners are elected. Won the May 19, 2026 Democratic primary with 55.7% over Angelia Pressley and Craig Cupid.
people.ideology: 'People Before Profits' Democrat aligned with the party's clean-energy and consumer wing; endorsed by Stacey Abrams, Andrew Young, Sierra Club Georgia, Georgia Conservation Voters, SACE Action Fund, Climate Cabinet Action, Georgia Working Families, Jane Fonda Climate PAC and numerous Democratic legislators.

positions.stance: Says 'The Commission must protect consumers from unnecessary rate increases' and aims to 'stop endless rate hikes'; says Georgians have 'shouldered the burden of repeated utility rate hikes' and that Georgia Power should be held accountable 'for every dollar it asks customers to pay' (2026).

Says data centers 'must pay the full cost of the infrastructure needed to serve them' rather than shift costs to homes and small businesses; calls for 'transparent, independent impact assessments' of air quality, water, energy demand, public health and grid reliability; said most data centers are heading to 'marginalized communities of mostly Black and brown people' (2026).
Wants Georgia Power to add more clean energy and expand its residential solar net-metering program, which she calls a 'win-win situation' (2026).
Calls for more transparency and accountability in PSC decisions: 'The public has a right to know who benefits, who pays, and who bears the consequences.'
Says a nearly $500 Georgia Power bill inspired her to run; focuses on 'working families and seniors on fixed incomes' and asks, 'How are they gonna afford this situation?' (2026).

Responding to rate increases driven by gas-plant construction, says families should not be 'forced to pay more and more every year for electricity'; has not stated a direct position on the 2025 IRP or the certified gas units.

Said of her Kennedy Space Center work, 'I was very highly involved with the technical side and understanding the engineering terminology,' while stopping short of claiming engineering work; the AJC says she helped with documentation after the Challenger disaster as a writer (April 2026 debate).

Calls to stop unnecessary rate hikes, says economic development should never come at expense of Georgia families, says will lower electric bills through greater accountability from Georgia Power, says data centers should pay their own way—not Georgia families, and says Georgia welcomes innovation but not at the expense of working families.
q: Stop unnecessary rate hikes.
Economic development should never come at the expense of Georgia families.

positions.stance: Says Georgia should require transparent impact assessments for data centers, says Georgians deserve truth about real cost of data centers, says need to understand impact of data centers on health and environment, says Georgia welcomes innovation but not at the expense of working families.
q: Before approving additional large-scale data centers, Georgia should require transparent, independent impact assessments that evaluate their effects on air quality, water resources, energy demand, public health, and the reliability of our electric grid.
Georgians deserve the truth about the real cost of data centers—not just in dollars, but in their impact on our health, our environment, and our communities.

positions.stance: Protects seniors, working families, veterans, and small businesses.
q: Protect seniors, working families, veterans, and small businesses.

people.name: Josh Tolbert
people.background: Republican nominee for the open PSC District 5 seat. A licensed professional engineer from Smyrna (Cobb County) with four engineering degrees from the University of Alabama (bachelor's 2009; master's degrees in mechanical engineering and in engineering science and mechanics, 2012; Ph.D. in mechanical engineering, 2015) and more than 15 years in power generation, spanning nuclear, coal, gas, biomass, geothermal and renewables. Former chief technology officer and VP of engineering at small-modular-reactor developer Last Energy, director of technology at the Energy Impact Center and CTO at Practical Steam; founded the consulting firm Atlanta Experts and works as an expert witness. Finished third (17.6%) in the November 2025 special election for State Senate District 35. Led the May 19, 2026 Republican primary with 47.2% and won the June 16 runoff over business owner Bobby Mehan 59.8%-40.2%.
people.ideology: Free-market, technocratic Republican: self-described 'pro-data center'; says stricter environmental laws 'often destroy jobs, raise costs, and weaken U.S. energy independence' and favors 'innovation and free-market solutions'; his campaign rejects 'costly mandates'; in SACE's multiple-choice survey he did not align with 'Climate change is real and requires urgent policy action.'

positions.stance: His chief concern is whether Georgia Power is overbuilding the grid for data centers; says a monopoly needs the commission to supply the 'consequences and feedback' competition would provide. In the April 2026 GOP debate he challenged a rival's no-rate-increase pledge as 'risking the reliability in certain areas.'

Calls himself 'pro-data center' for the economic opportunity but warned the PSC at a December 2025 public hearing about financial risks to the public from overbuilding for data centers; pledges 'I will ensure costs are allocated to those who cause them — not shifted onto ratepayers' and supports cost-causation principles so data centers pay the generation, transmission and distribution costs their demand creates.

Says he likes nuclear technology but 'I hate the price of nuclear power we built,' citing Vogtle at 'almost $17 million a megawatt' versus $1-2 million for conventional plants; would back future nuclear only with strict cost controls and overruns borne by private investors, and blames federal regulation for the cost (2026).
Calls gas 'the most dependable, affordable base-load source' for growing demand and lists 'secure natural gas delivery' as part of reliable service (2026).

Says 'I support Georgians to have opportunities for distributed power, including solar power'; says every energy source, including renewables, should be used only where its engineering and economics make sense, and his campaign rejects 'costly mandates' (2026).
Wants commissioners to explain their votes to the public and says he would ask technical questions of witnesses: 'I would like to be the nerd on your team' (April 2026).
'Utility decisions must be built on engineering, not forecasts that miss the mark'; pledges to 'scrutinize proposals, challenge unsupported claims, and ensure only justified costs are passed on.'

signals.claim: Would likely support additional gas-fired capacity in the 2028 IRP while pressing Georgia Power on load forecasts.
signals.basis: His statements that gas is the most dependable base-load source and his concern about overbuilding for forecasted data-center demand.

signals.claim: Would likely back stronger cost-causation and stranded-cost provisions in large-load contracts.
signals.basis: His campaign pledge on allocating costs to those who cause them and his Dec. 2025 PSC testimony on overbuilding risk.

signals.claim: Would likely oppose ratepayer recovery of cost overruns on any future nuclear project.
signals.basis: His statements that nuclear overruns should be borne by private investors and his criticism of Vogtle's per-megawatt cost.

people.name: Amanda Hollowell
people.background: Savannah-based political organizer making her first run for office. She is Chief of Campaigns at Color Of Change and previously directed national organizing at When We All Vote and led advocacy campaigns at the Georgia Budget and Policy Institute and 9to5 Georgia; she has served on the boards of Reform Georgia, the League of Women Voters of Coastal Georgia and the Georgia Alliance for Social Justice and on Savannah's Black Heritage Festival Committee. Born in Palm Springs, California, she holds a bachelor's degree from UC Berkeley (2001) and says she has organized in the region for nearly two decades; she comes from a military family and describes herself as a full-time caregiver to her veteran father. She finished second in the eight-candidate May 19, 2026 Democratic primary (24.7%) and won the June 16 runoff over Joyce Marie Griggs, 53.0% to 47.0%.
people.ideology: Progressive, organizer-wing Democrat: endorsed by the Working Families Party, Black Voters Matter Action PAC, The Collective PAC and Higher Heights for America PAC, with a Moms Demand Action Gun Sense Candidate distinction; says "Healthcare is a human right" and wants "a tax system that rewards work, not just wealth."

positions.stance: Supports Medicaid expansion and lowering out-of-pocket costs ("Healthcare is a human right, and I will work to protect it"); supports postpartum Medicaid expansion and opposes cuts to Medicaid and SNAP (Oct. 2026).
Wants to fully fund public schools, support teachers, expand universal pre-K and invest in higher education and apprenticeship programs to keep graduates in the region; opposes education cuts.
Wants to raise wages, expand affordable housing, direct federal resources to Southeast Georgia and support small and mid-sized businesses, citing the ports, tourism and manufacturing.

Supports the John R. Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act, the Freedom to Vote Act, the Native American Voting Rights Act and the Unhoused VOTE Act; says she wants residents to have access to the ballot.
Opposes data centers that do not create enough jobs and says the region should not accept the first corporate offer; wants investments to benefit everyone (Oct. 2026).

Wants to protect service members' benefits during and after service and address veterans' housing shortages and the transition to civilian life, citing concerns raised by VFW and American Legion members.
Called the U.S. military action in Iran an unconstitutional war and said the U.S. should return to negotiations, noting effects on farmers, manufacturing and grocery prices (Oct. 2026).
Received Moms Demand Action's Gun Sense Candidate distinction, which the group tied to her support for "common-sense gun safety policies" (Apr. 2026).
Supports extending paid family leave for state employees.

Will host a community gathering focused on healing and awareness for sexual assault survivors and says “Together in Care” is a space to stand together and show community commitment to care and respect.
q: On Thursday, April 23, 2026, Amanda Hollowell will be joined by community leaders for “Together In Care: A Sexual Assault Awareness Month Event,” a community gathering and press conference focused on healing, support, and awareness for survivors.
“Together in Care” is a space to stand together, uplift voices, and show that our community is committed to care and respect.

people.name: Sanford Bishop
people.background: Albany Democrat who has represented Southwest Georgia's 2nd District since January 1993 (first elected Nov. 1992) and sought an 18th term in 2026. Born in Mobile, Alabama in 1947, he graduated from Morehouse College (1968) and Emory University School of Law (1971), served in the U.S. Army (1969-71) and practiced law in Columbus, where he lived from 1972 to 1996. He served in the Georgia House (1977-1990) and Georgia Senate (1991-92) before Congress. He has sat on the House Appropriations Committee since 2003 and is the ranking Democrat on its Agriculture-Rural Development-FDA subcommittee, with seats on the Military Construction-VA and Financial Services-General Government subcommittees; he was a senior Democratic whip in the 112th and 113th Congresses.
people.ideology: Moderate, agriculture- and military-focused Democrat: member of the Blue Dog Coalition, senior member of the Congressional Black Caucus, No Labels Problem Solvers participant, co-founder of the Congressional Military Family Caucus and co-chair of the Peanut Caucus; votes with Democrats on major party-line measures while backing bipartisan funding deals.

positions.stance: Voted no on H.R. 1, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (July 3, 2025), which extended the 2017 tax cuts while cutting future Medicaid and SNAP spending.

Voted no on the Nov. 12, 2025 bill ending the fall 2025 shutdown, saying it did not adequately support Georgians who rely on ACA subsidies; voted yes on a bipartisan Sept. 2026 stopgap funding agencies at FY2026 levels through Dec. 11, 2026 (passed 370-48).

Cited inadequate support for Georgians relying on Affordable Care Act subsidies in opposing the Nov. 2025 funding bill; opposes proposed service reductions at Robins Air Force Base's 78th Medical Group, which he ties to health care access.

Voted no on the House FY2027 NDAA (H.R. 8800, passed 216-212, July 2026), saying GOP leaders added "unrelated, divisive provisions," while backing Fort Benning modernization, Robins AFB and a 5-7% military pay raise.
Objected to combining the NDAA with the SAVE America Act, which he described as "unrelated election legislation that would prevent millions of American citizens from voting" (July 2026).

Ranking Democrat on the Agriculture-FDA appropriations subcommittee and Peanut Caucus co-chair; co-introduced the National 4-H Week resolution (Oct. 2026) and announced $20 million in longleaf pine restoration grants (June 2026).
Co-leads, with Republican Rep. Austin Scott, H.R. 9416, the Ocmulgee Mounds National Park Redesignation Act to create Georgia's first national park (hearing July 2026).
Applauded a June 2026 federal court ruling blocking the Trump administration's $100,000 visa fee.

Voted against the FY2027 National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs appropriations bill, saying it "will lead to the continued erosion of American diplomacy," and against a Massie amendment barring funds in it for Israel and for humanitarian aid in Gaza, which he said "jeopardizes the investment we need in regional missile defense" (July 2026).
Lead House sponsor of the Hiring Heroes Act (signed 2011) and sponsor of the Disabled Veterans Tax Termination Act; co-founded the Congressional Military Family Caucus.

people.record: 119th Congress: voted no on H.R. 1 (July 2025), no on the Nov. 2025 shutdown-ending CR, yes on the Sept. 2026 CR (370-48), and no on the House FY2027 NDAA H.R. 8800 (July 2026); co-leads H.R. 9416 (Ocmulgee Mounds National Park) with Rep. Austin Scott and co-introduced the National 4-H Week resolution (Oct. 2026). Ranking Democrat on the Agriculture-Rural Development-FDA appropriations subcommittee. Ran unopposed in the May 2026 Democratic primary (72,498 votes).

signals.basis: Blue Dog Coalition membership (official bio), his yes vote on the Sept. 2026 bipartisan stopgap (370-48), and his statement that the bill "reasserts Congress's Constitutional authority to direct funding and check the Executive Branch" and removes "the immediate threat of a shutdown."

signals.basis: Ranking role on Agriculture appropriations, Peanut Caucus co-chair, and his no vote on H.R. 1's SNAP changes.

signals.claim: Would likely support a final FY2027 NDAA if the SAVE America Act and other riders are removed.
signals.basis: His July 2026 statement that the riders made 'this version' impossible to support while pledging to protect Georgia military priorities.

Nikema Williams (Mar. 2025). Rules Committee member; chair of the Small Business Subcommittee on Innovation, Entrepreneurship and Workforce Development.

people.name: Maura Keller
people.background: Retired U.S. Army lieutenant colonel and former Atlanta VA health care worker from Fayetteville (Fayette County), where she has lived about 28 years. Born in South Weymouth, Massachusetts, she enlisted in the Army as a military police officer in 1978, became an officer, received the General Douglas MacArthur Leadership Award and retired in 2004 after 26 years; she then worked as a Defense Department contractor on military efficiency projects before moving into health care. She was the 2024 Democratic nominee in the 3rd District, losing to Brian Jack by roughly 2-to-1, and won the May 19, 2026 Democratic primary with 60.8% over George Melville Johnson.
people.ideology: Mainstream, labor- and veteran-aligned Democrat: endorsed by the Georgia AFL-CIO, Veterans For Responsible Leadership and Common Defense; recognized by Moms Demand Action; emphasizes nonpartisan service ("Take the Democrat, Republican, all that away") and practical solutions over partisan positioning.

positions.stance: Says "costs are too high" and that teachers and first responders cannot afford to live where they work; supports raising the minimum wage, higher-paying jobs and lower costs at the pump (2026).
Raises concerns about long-term solvency and possible benefit reductions without changes; her campaign site commits to "fixing social security."
Says constituents report insurance premiums that have "almost double[d]" and uncertainty about coverage; campaign focuses on rural hospital closures and shrinking coverage ("We deserve basic care").
Calls housing affordability a dominant issue in the district and notes seniors lack downsizing options (Apr. 2026).
Says the region needs data centers but has concerns about placing them in rural and agricultural areas: "They just don't have to be in your backyard" (Apr. 2026).
Supports Right to Repair laws for farmers, which she says are "sitting unpassed in the House."
Campaign priority to "end food and housing scarcity" among veterans and protect veteran care and benefits programs.
Campaign says she will work to stop corruption "from the White House on down."
Listed by Moms Demand Action as a recognized candidate (2026).

Supports Trans people being left alone and High School sports not being political; supports access to American dream regardless of sexual orientation, gender, or skin color; promises to never vote against those who need representation.

Maura offers unwavering support for all and believes that every citizen should have access to the American dream, regardless of sexual orientation, gender, or skin color.

positions.stance: Would demand stronger Social Security payments to keep pace with inflation; would work across the aisle to ensure real reform for seniors; believes soaring costs force seniors to choose between medical treatment and other essentials.
q: Maura will demand stronger Social Security payments that keep pace with inflation to ensure every senior lives a healthy, fulfilling life.
At the same time, she will work across the aisle to ensure real reform, because she will not risk letting seniors live without getting what they paid in.

positions.stance: Would push for stronger enforcement to stop illegal immigration and streamline legal pathways; believes we need to protect our border and prevent people with criminal records from crossing; believes we should treat people humanely, deport if needed, and provide citizenship pathway.

I believe we need to protect our border and prevent people with criminal records from crossing into our country, especially violent criminals.

positions.stance: Believes discussion on issues like inflation, job losses, and healthcare cuts is more important; voted to create biggest deficit, cut healthcare by $1 Trillion, and extend Iran War; believes looking at payroll tax and income caps will help make ends meet.
q: I actually believe this entire discussion is a distraction from issues like inflation, job losses, and healthcare cuts.

In his first term as a Congressman, he helped create the biggest deficit in American history, cut healthcare by $1 Trillion (the largest ever in American history), and voted to extend the Iran War three times.

people.name: Austin Scott
people.background: Republican U.S. representative for Georgia's 8th District (Middle and South Georgia from Macon to the Florida line) since January 2011 and the longest-serving member of the state's Republican congressional delegation; won a ninth term on November 3, 2026. Based in Tifton; born in Augusta in 1969; B.B.A. in risk management and insurance from the University of Georgia (1993); ran an insurance brokerage for about 20 years. Served in the Georgia House 1996–2011 (first elected at 26, chaired Governmental Affairs), briefly ran for governor in 2009–10, then unseated Democrat Jim Marshall in 2010. In the 119th Congress he is vice chair of the Agriculture Committee (chairing its General Farm Commodities, Risk Management and Credit subcommittee), chairs the Intelligence Committee's National Intelligence Enterprise subcommittee, and sits on Armed Services and Rules.

orig.background: Republican U.S. representative for Georgia's 8th District (Middle and South Georgia from Macon to the Florida line) since January 2011 and the longest-serving member of the state's Republican congressional delegation; won a ninth term on November 3, 2026. Based in Tifton; born in Augusta in 1969; B.B.A. in risk management and insurance from the University of Georgia (1993); ran an insurance brokerage for about 20 years. Served in the Georgia House 1996–2011 (first elected at 26, chaired Governmental Affairs), briefly ran for governor in 2009–10, then unseated Democrat Jim Marshall in 2010. In the 119th Congress he is vice chair of the Agriculture Committee (chairing its General Farm Commodities, Risk Management and Credit subcommittee), chairs the Intelligence Committee's National Intelligence Enterprise subcommittee, and sits on Armed Services and Rules.
orig.record: 119th Congress sponsorships include H.R. 8322 (FISA title VII extension, enacted as Public Law 119-84, April 2026); H.R. 8884, the Removing Barriers to Work for Disabled Americans Act (passed the House in July 2026); H.R. 2345 and H.R. 9416 to redesignate Ocmulgee Mounds as a national park and preserve (with Rep. Sanford Bishop); H.R. 9933, South Atlantic Red Snapper Fair Access Act; H.R. 7559 (outsourcing deduction); H.R. 7120, Purple Heart Freedom to Work Act; H.R. 8863 (ATF employees' fire-protection pay); and H.R. 6598 (CFTC R&D modernization), plus numerous Rules Committee resolutions. Key votes: Yea on H.R. 1, the SAVE Act, the Laken Riley Act, H.R. 5371, the Epstein Files Transparency Act, the No Rogue Rulings Act (H.R. 1526), H.R. 875 and H.R. 28; Nay on the GENIUS Act. In October 2023 he ran for Speaker, losing to Jim Jordan 81–124 in the GOP conference vote.

people.name: Kelly Esti
people.background: Democratic nominee in Georgia's 8th District. A U.S. Navy veteran (1999–2002, nuclear-trained sailor) who works as an analyst for Delta Air Lines after roles at E*Trade, JPMorgan Chase and UPS; holds a Ph.D. in public policy (Walden University, 2018), an MBA (Webster University, 2007) and a bachelor's in management (Ottawa University, 2006). Grew up in Magnolia, in rural southern Mississippi; lives in Hapeville in metro Atlanta, outside the district, and told WALB in April 2026 he had been 'showing up in the district since September.' Civic roles include the Fulton County zoning board, the Hapeville Board of Appeals, the board of the charter school Main Street Academy, helping found the city of South Fulton, and legislative chair for Georgia Equality. Won the May 19, 2026 Democratic primary over Worth County school board member Justin Lucas, 53.5%–46.5%.
people.ideology: Progressive-leaning Democrat: calls for removing the president from office, higher taxes on wealthy individuals and large multinational corporations, and a statewide passenger-rail line; has served as legislative chair of the LGBTQ-rights group Georgia Equality; the endorsements he lists come from state Reps. Floyd Griffin and Tanya Miller and two small-town mayors.

positions.stance: Wants lower everyday and health-care costs for families and young single adults; told WALB (April 2026) his mother's costs are rising 'because the ACA has been stripped away.' His campaign site calls health care 'a Public Good.'

Proposes the 'Georgia Intrastate Transit (The GIT),' a passenger rail line linking major cities 'from Valdosta to Chattanooga with stops along the way' (WALB); says it would reduce road wear, congestion, pollution and accidents and let growth spread beyond Atlanta.

Says he is 'most passionate about education and transportation' and calls education 'the cornerstone at keeping the US healthy'; would fund education partly through higher taxes on the wealthy and large corporations; his site calls education 'a PUBLIC GOOD.'
Named removing the president from office and jailing him as his top priority, adding, 'And he's also a felon' (WALB, April 2026).

Urges young people to vote, tells people with past felony convictions 'no, you can vote,' and proposes civic-engagement centers in place of traditional congressional offices to teach constituents about civics and voting (WALB, April 2026).
Pledges regular town halls ('I cannot represent you if I'm not listening to you') and said Austin Scott 'has not held a town hall since 2013' (WALB).
Blames rising costs on federal spending under Trump ('he's printing and printing and printing') and says 'we have to get into a place where people can afford life again' (WALB, April 2026).

Would support federal programs like VA health care, disability benefits, education support, and housing assistance for veterans, would oversee the federal agencies that support veterans and military communities, and supports service members, veterans, and their families receiving earned support.
q: Veterans in our district rely on federal programs like VA health care, disability benefits, education support, and housing assistance.
As a member of Congress, part of my job would be to oversee the federal agencies that support veterans and military communities.

positions.stance: Would have communities explore renewable energy alternatives if they believe they will reduce long-term costs.
q: As renewable energy, like solar and wind, becomes more affordable nationwide, communities should have the option to explore these alternatives if they believe they will reduce long‑term costs.

positions.stance: Spearheaded opposition to Religious Freedom Bill (2015).
q: Spearheaded successful opposition to Religious Freedom Bill (2015)

positions.stance: Believes affordable learning of new skills strengthens families and supports economic stability.
q: When people can afford to learn new skills, it strengthens families and supports long‑term economic stability across the region.

positions.stance: Saw how unreliable basic services can set back a community.
q: Growing up in the South, I saw how easily a community can be set back when basic services are unreliable.

positions.stance: Focus is on giving cities and counties tools to choose what works best for them.
q: My focus is on giving each city and county the tools they need to choose what works best for them.

positions.stance: Ensures federal protections are enforced, agencies follow the law, and fair treatment for all.
q: As your congressman, my responsibility is to make sure federal protections are enforced consistently, agencies follow the law, and everyone in the district (no matter their background) can rely on fair treatment when dealing with federal programs.

positions.stance: Protected community from careless developers and/or destructive corporate interests.
q: Protected the community from careless developers and/or destructive corporate interests

people.name: Andrew Clyde
people.background: Republican U.S. representative for Georgia's 9th District (northeast Georgia; all or parts of 12 counties, including Hall, Jackson and Gwinnett) since January 2021; won a fourth term on November 3, 2026 after beating two local-official primary challengers with 76%. Born 1963 in Walkerton, Ontario, Canada, and raised in Indiana and New York; B.B.A. from Bethel University and an MBA from UGA's Terry College of Business (1999). Served 28 years in the Navy (active duty 1985–96), including three combat deployments to Iraq and Kuwait, retiring as a commander in 2013. Founded the firearms retailer Clyde Armory, which began as a hobby business in his garage in 1991, and opened a second location in Warner Robins in 2014. A 2013 IRS civil-forfeiture seizure of $940,000 (later reversed, with $900,000 refunded) made him an advocate for forfeiture reform; the Clyde-Hirsch-Sowers RESPECT Act became law in 2019 as part of the Taxpayer First Act. Lives in unincorporated Jackson County. Serves on Appropriations and Budget.
people.ideology: Freedom Caucus conservative: member of the House Freedom Caucus and the Republican Study Committee; declines to take part in the earmark process; advocates the FairTax and abolishing the IRS, the Department of Education and the EPA; Trump-endorsed in 2026 and describes himself as an 'America First Representative.' His 2026 primary challengers, then-Gainesville Mayor Sam Couvillon and Hall County Commissioner Gregg Poole, criticized him for not bringing federal earmark funding to the district; Eagle Forum called him 'a fighter for fiscal sanity.'

positions.stance: Calls the Second Amendment 'the teeth in "We the People"' that 'must never be compromised by the government'; filed an amicus brief in defense of Second Amendment rights (Sept. 2026 release); made House floor remarks in May 2026 on H.R. 1041, a bill to 'restore veterans' rights to own or possess firearms'; co-sponsored a 2023 bill to designate the AR-15-style rifle as the national gun.

Supports replacing the income tax with the FairTax (H.R. 25) and dismantling the IRS; warns of a sovereign-debt crisis and refuses earmarks ('It's money spent outside the Constitution, and it's wrong'); voted against the 2023 debt-limit deal; initially opposed the 2025 reconciliation bill with Freedom Caucus allies over the pace of green-energy phase-outs, then voted Yea on H.R. 1.

Pro-life; says 'life begins at conception and ends at natural death'; made floor remarks in Jan. 2026 on the 'Day of Tears' resolution (H.Res. 56), the March for Life and the Roe v. Wade anniversary; in 2013 donated a 5,000-square-foot facility to Mercy Health Center and Athens Crisis Pregnancy Center.

Introduced H.R. 8460 (April 2026) to repeal Temporary Protected Status authority and the 'MAGA Act' (H.R. 10377, Sept. 2026) to exclude noncitizens from census apportionment counts and require a citizenship question; voted for the Laken Riley Act (S. 5) and H.R. 875; made floor remarks in March 2026 on FY2026 Homeland Security appropriations (H.R. 7147), including CBP and ICE funding.

Voted for the SAVE Act (H.R. 22, 2025); voted on Jan. 6, 2021 against certifying Arizona's and Pennsylvania's electors; his release says the MAGA Act would 'Safeguard U.S. Elections & Representation'; spoke in Feb. 2026 on H.R. 7296 to require proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.
Introduced H.R. 9453 (June 2026) to preserve consumer vehicle choice and limit Clean Air Act regulation; pushed in 2025 for faster repeal of clean-energy tax credits.
Says the Department of Education and the EPA 'must go,' with functions returned to the states; federal programs outside enumerated powers 'should be eliminated.'
'There is no one more supportive of President Trump's agenda than me' (Sept. 2025); Trump endorsed him for 2026.

Introduced H.Res. 1351 (June 9, 2026) to impeach U.S. District Judge Eleanor L. Ross; voted for the No Rogue Rulings Act (H.R. 1526, 2025) limiting injunctions that reach beyond the parties to a case; in Jan. 2026 sought to strike salary and expense funding for the staffs of U.S. District Judges James E. Boasberg and Deborah L. Boardman during appropriations debate.
Pledges to make veterans' care 'a top priority'; voted against the 2022 PACT Act (H.R. 3967) on toxic-exposure benefits.

In May 2021 said video of the Capitol attack resembled 'a normal tourist visit' while acknowledging he helped barricade the House chamber door; voted against Congressional Gold Medals for Capitol police (2021).

Says he helped persuade the Army Corps of Engineers to reverse some Lake Lanier park closures and is pushing legislation to let local governments lease parks (2025; challenger Gregg Poole credited Rep. Mike Collins for addressing the closures); says his office has resolved 3,000 constituent cases.
Supports the Clyde-Hirsh-Sowers RESPECT Act.
q: Three times in three different Congressional terms, Congress unanimously passed the Clyde-Hirsh-Sowers RESPECT Act.

people.record: House Freedom Caucus member; 79 bills as primary sponsor over his career (Legisletter count). In 2025–26 he introduced H.R. 8460 (repeal TPS authority), H.R. 9453 (vehicle choice / Clean Air Act limits), H.R. 10377 (the 'MAGA Act' on apportionment and a census citizenship question, introduced with more than 40 House Republicans) and H.Res. 1351 (impeachment of Judge Eleanor L. Ross). Key 119th Congress votes: Yea on H.R. 1 (after initial opposition), the SAVE Act, the Laken Riley Act, H.R. 5371 (ending the 2025 shutdown), the GENIUS Act, the Epstein Files Transparency Act, the No Rogue Rulings Act and H.R. 28. Earlier: Nay on the 2023 Fiscal Responsibility Act, the 2022 PACT Act, the 2021 Juneteenth holiday bill (the AJC reported he objected to its title) and the March 2021 Congressional Gold Medal bill for police who defended the Capitol (H.R. 1085); voted against certifying two states' 2020 electors. Declines to take part in the earmark process.

signals.basis: Owns a firearms retailer; says the Second Amendment 'must never be compromised by the government'; filed a Second Amendment amicus brief in 2026.

people.name: Caitlyn Gegen
people.background: Democratic nominee in Georgia's 9th District. A Suwanee resident and community organizer who says she has lived in the district most of her life; a UGA 'Double Dawg' (bachelor's in international relations and master of public administration, 2021) with a further master's from the London School of Economics (2022), and a HOPE Scholarship recipient whose parents taught in Gwinnett County Public Schools. Worked on the 2018 Chalis Montgomery congressional campaign, co-organized a protest at UGA against the state's 'Heartbeat Bill' abortion law, lobbied members of Congress on arms-sales policy and cites experience in local government. Announced in February 2026 and won the May 19 Democratic primary over Nick Alex, 60%–40%.

Criticizes the president for having 'started an endless war' and for 'threatening voter intimidation in the upcoming election' (2026 questionnaire).
Lists women's rights, LGBTQ+ rights, due process and voting rights as human-rights priorities.

people.name: Houston Gaines
people.background: Republican representative-elect for Georgia's 10th District (Athens and counties in central Georgia just east of metro Atlanta), the seat Rep. Mike Collins left to run for the U.S. Senate. Born and raised in Athens; University of Georgia graduate; works with Carter Engineering, an Oconee County small business. Elected to the Georgia House in 2018 at age 23, defeating Democratic incumbent Deborah Gonzalez in HD-117 after losing a 2017 special election to her; re-elected in 2020, 2022 and 2024, representing HD-120 since 2023. Vice chair of the House Appropriations Committee (named January 2025), vice chairman of the House Majority Caucus (elected November 2024) and chair of a 2024 House study committee on nicotine vapor products. Won the May 19, 2026 primary outright with 66.9% over film executive Ryan Millsap, who pledged to self-fund, and Jeff Baker; he was 30 when he entered the race.
people.ideology: Leadership-aligned conservative Republican running on Trump's agenda: received Trump's 'Complete and Total Endorsement' (April 15, 2026) plus endorsements from Speaker Mike Johnson, Majority Leader Steve Scalise, Whip Tom Emmer, Jim Jordan and Rich McCormick; vice chairman of the Georgia House Majority Caucus. Athens' Flagpole wrote that 'since being elected in 2018, though, Gaines has shifted far to the right.'

positions.stance: Campaign plank 'Deport criminal illegals'; his site says 'His legislation ensured total cooperation with ICE' and 'Deportations must continue, and the border must stay secure.' Flagpole lists among his state record measures requiring local law enforcement to cooperate more closely with ICE after the murder of Laken Riley.
Says he 'voted for the Heartbeat Bill' and will join President Trump and Congress to 'defund planned parenthood'; a local vote tracker records his yes vote on the 2019 abortion ban.
Says the Second Amendment 'means exactly what it says: "shall not be infringed"'; voted for Georgia's 2022 permitless-carry law and a 2025 firearm safe-storage measure (local vote tracker).

'Restore fiscal sanity': says he 'has supported a balanced budget every year – while cutting taxes at a record level' and calls to 'cut spending and cut taxes'; vice chair of the Georgia House Appropriations Committee since January 2025.

'Crack down on crime'; says he 'led the charge to stop the "defund the police" movement in Georgia.' Flagpole lists among his state record measures requiring cash bail for minor offenses after the Athens-Clarke Commission eliminated it and creating an agency to oversee 'rogue prosecutors' after the election of District Attorney Deborah Gonzalez; sponsored HB 231 (2021), which FOX 5 described as filling a gap in Georgia's domestic-violence law.

A local vote tracker records yes votes on school-voucher bills in 2021, 2023 and 2024, the 2023 ban on gender-affirming treatment for minors and the 2025 ban on transgender girls in girls' sports; campaign plank 'Crush woke ideology'; says he 'voted to stop taxpayer funds from paying for sex change surgeries.'
Served as secretary of the Georgia House Health Committee (2021–22); voted for postpartum Medicaid coverage extensions (2020, 2022) and to apply for Medicaid waivers (2019).
Voted for Georgia's 2021 omnibus election law and for 2022 and 2024 election-administration changes (local vote tracker, which gives no bill numbers).
'Make American made': promote American manufacturing and oppose outsourcing.
'Support our farmers'; opposes Chinese Communist Party ownership of U.S. farmland.
'Promote peace through strength': 'The way to peace is through strength.'
Co-sponsored Georgia's version of the GENIUS Act on stablecoins; campaign plank 'Supporting digital assets.'
'Restore ethics to Congress'; supports ending insider trading by members of Congress.
Frames his run as taking 'the fight to Washington' in support of President Trump's agenda; Trump endorsed him April 15, 2026 as an 'Eighth-Generation Georgian.'

Pushing for the death penalty in the UGA murder case, bans no-cash bail for both violent and non-violent crimes and says legislation will make it clear Georgia is not going down the path of other states that have allowed no-cash bail.
q: Georgia State Rep. Houston Gaines joined 'America's Newsroom' to discuss why he is pushing for the death penalty in the UGA murder case after the Athens DA tapped a special prosecutor to handle the case.

The ban on no-cash bail applies to both violent and non-violent crimes, from murder and rape to possession of marijuana with intent to distribute and white-collar crimes including forgery and financial transaction card fraud.

positions.stance: Calls for new efforts to bring accountability to local prosecutors.
q: Houston Gaines and Joseph Gullett comes after Gov. Brian Kemp and Lt. Gov. Burt Jones called for new efforts to bring “accountability” to local prosecutors.

people.record: Seven-plus years in the Georgia House (2019–Jan. 2027): vice chair of Appropriations (named January 2025), House Majority Caucus vice chairman (elected November 2024), chair of the 2024 House Study Committee on Safety and Consumer Protection of Nicotine Vapor Products, and sponsor of HB 231 (2021, domestic violence); Trump's endorsement post, quoted by The Center Square, credits him with 'authoring more than 20 bills that have passed the Georgia Legislature.' A local vote tracker records yes votes on the 2019 abortion ban, 2022 permitless carry, voucher bills (2021, 2023, 2024), the 2021 election overhaul, the 2023 minors' gender-care ban and the 2025 transgender sports ban, as well as postpartum Medicaid extensions and a 2025 firearm safe-storage measure.

signals.basis: Endorsed by Johnson, Scalise and Emmer; state Appropriations vice chair and caucus leadership role.

signals.claim: Likely to support federal school-choice tax credits or voucher programs.
signals.basis: Three yes votes on Georgia voucher legislation (2021, 2023, 2024).

signals.claim: Likely to back federal digital-asset and stablecoin frameworks.
signals.basis: Co-sponsored Georgia's GENIUS-style stablecoin bill; campaign plank on digital assets.

signals.claim: Likely to co-sponsor a congressional stock-trading ban.
signals.basis: Campaign plank on ending insider trading by members.

signals.claim: Possible sponsorship of federal measures on bail, prosecutor accountability or sanctuary-jurisdiction penalties.
signals.basis: State record on cash bail, 'rogue prosecutor' oversight and local ICE cooperation (Flagpole).

people.name: Rick W. Allen
people.background: Republican U.S. representative for Georgia's 12th District (east Georgia, including Augusta) since January 2015; won a seventh term on November 3, 2026 after an 83% primary win over Tori Branum. people.ideology: Conservative Republican whom the AJC calls a 'faithful member of the U.S. House's Republican majority' who votes consistently for bills backed by Trump and House leaders; voted to reject Arizona's and Pennsylvania's 2020 electors; Trump-endorsed in 2022 and 2026; a social conservative who voted against the 2022 Respect for Marriage Act and co-sponsored a 2015 resolution for a constitutional amendment to ban same-sex marriage.

positions.stance: Voted for the 2017 tax law, H.R. 1 (the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act) and the FY2025 budget resolution; called for a balanced budget amendment in his 2014 campaign; in 2025 spoke approvingly of ending the carried-interest loophole.

Campaigned in 2014 on repealing the ACA; introduced H.R. 9798 (July 2026) to exempt certain ERISA employer plans from ACA essential-health-benefit rules and H.R. 7895 (March 2026) to prohibit kickbacks to pharmacy benefit managers; secured Sections 704–705 of the FY27 NDAA (H.R. 8800) to halt planned changes at Eisenhower Army Medical Center at Fort Gordon.

Chairs the Education and Workforce Committee's HELP subcommittee; his Retire through Ownership Act (S. 2403) passed the House in September 2026 and was signed into law in October 2026 (his Oct. 16 release says Trump signed it 'yesterday'); demanded answers from American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten (July 7, 2026); has proposed legislation to curb environmental, social and governance (ESG) investing.

Campaigned in 2014 on more local control of education; voted against the 2022 Mental Health Matters Act, saying it 'will only benefit trial lawyers'; hosted an Education and Workforce Committee field hearing in Augusta in July 2026.
Voted for the Laken Riley Act (S. 5, 2025); supported the 2017 travel-ban executive order.

Voted for the SAVE Act (H.R. 22, 2025); on Jan. 6–7, 2021 voted to reject Arizona's and Pennsylvania's electors and signed the Texas v. Pennsylvania amicus brief; the AJC says he 'shared unverified conspiracy theories' after the 2020 election.

Campaigned in 2014 for more domestic drilling and has supported the MOX fuel facility at the Savannah River Site; supported a 2025 freeze of Inflation Reduction Act funds; in 2026 made floor remarks on bills to limit new DOE energy-conservation standards (H.R. 4626) and bar DOE from enforcing efficiency standards for manufactured housing (H.R. 5184), and on H.R. 6398 on EPA review under the Clean Air Act.

Voted against the 2022 Respect for Marriage Act; in 2015 co-sponsored a resolution to amend the Constitution to ban same-sex marriage; in 2023 opposed Tom Emmer for Speaker over Emmer's past support for same-sex couples' protections.
Endorsed by Trump in 2026; voted for the administration's 2025 reconciliation law and the H.R. 5371 continuing resolution ending the 2025 shutdown.
Introduced H.R. 7195 (Jan. 2026) to provide USDA financial assistance to forest-product harvesting and hauling businesses hit by major market disruption.
Touts a $13.6 million VA grant (Sept. 2026) for a veterans cemetery in Augusta funded through H.R. 5371.
Voted against a 2023 Ukraine security-aid bill; voted to support Israel after the October 2023 Hamas attack.

people.background: Democratic representative-elect for Georgia's 13th District for the full term beginning January 2027. people.background: Republican U.S. representative for Georgia's 14th District since April 14, 2026, after winning the April 7 special runoff (55.9%) to finish Marjorie Taylor Greene's term; re-elected to a full term November 3 after an 81% primary. Born Clayton McLean Fuller in 1981 in Brazoria, Texas, and raised in Helen, Georgia; B.A. in English literature from Emory, M.P.A. from Cornell, J.D. from SMU and a Master of Military Art and Science from Air Command and Staff College. Air Force JAG officer 2010–14, later rising to lieutenant colonel in the Air National Guard, with a six-month 2024 deployment to Kuwait as a legal adviser supporting U.S. Central Command; White House Fellow 2018–19 in the Office of the Vice President and with the Defense Department; assistant district attorney and then, by Gov. Kemp's appointment (March 2023), district attorney of the Lookout Mountain Judicial Circuit until resigning effective Jan. 12, 2026 to run. Placed fourth in the 2020 GA-14 primary. people.name: Shawn Harris
people.background: Democratic nominee in Georgia's 14th District for the second cycle running. A retired Army National Guard brigadier general with about 40 years in uniform, beginning as an enlisted Marine and including an infantry command in Afghanistan; agribusiness degree from Tuskegee University and a graduate degree from the Army War College. Born in Blakely, where he grew up around peanut farming; now runs a cow-calf operation (Red Angus, Angus and Charolais) on family land in Cedartown, and AP says he lives on his cattle farm in Rockmart. Lost to Marjorie Taylor Greene in 2024 (35.6%); in the 2026 special election to replace Greene he led the crowded March 10 first round with 37.3% before losing the April 7 runoff to Clay Fuller 44.1%–55.9%; unopposed in the May 19 Democratic primary. Raised about $8.4 million in the 2026 cycle, drawing national attention and a Pete Buttigieg campaign visit.

people.name: Ben Watson
people.background: Republican state senator for District 1 (all of Bryan and Liberty counties and most of Chatham County) since January 2015, after two terms in the Georgia House (elected 2010 from Savannah's islands district). A primary-care physician who has practiced internal medicine and geriatrics in Savannah since 1988; a native of Twin City, Ga.; educated at the University of Georgia and the Medical College of Georgia. In the 2025-2026 Senate he chairs the Health and Human Services Committee and the Appropriations Subcommittee on Health and Human Development and is vice chairman of the Rules Committee; he also chaired HHS in 2019-2022 and the Reapportionment and Redistricting Committee in 2017. He was unopposed in the May 2026 Republican primary.
people.ideology: Mainstream conservative Republican within the Senate's committee leadership: chairs Health and Human Services and is Rules vice chair, is listed among the sponsors of SB 1 (2025), and campaigns on income-tax cuts and public safety. No Freedom Caucus affiliation or primary challenge found.

positions.stance: Says Georgia's taxes are low; told WTOC in October 2026 he wants to cut the state income tax 'at least in half' and is already working on property taxes. His campaign site credits him with helping pass the income-tax cut from 6.0% to 5.5% with a doubled standard deduction.

As HHS chairman says Georgia is 'falling behind' other states in physicians and nurses per capita. Sponsored SB 247 (2026, passed), which creates a provisional license for internationally trained physicians who practice under supervision in rural counties, hospitals or federally qualified health centers, with a path to full licensure after four years plus two more years in underserved areas; earlier sponsored SB 16, the Interstate Medical Licensure Compact Act.
His campaign site says he supported SB 106, which authorized Georgia to seek Medicaid and Affordable Care Act waivers, and that the waivers increase access and lower premiums.
Calls public safety 'the number one role of government' and credits GBI involvement against gang activity under Gov. Kemp (October 2026).
Says 'affordability is a huge issue in our society' and names housing costs and property taxes as the concerns he hears most from voters (October 2026).

Sponsored HB 445 amending the Shore Protection Act to define 'dynamic dune field' and specify where construction may be permitted landward of dunes; voted for legislation protecting estuarine areas and allowing oyster farming.

As HHS chairman in 2022 he carried Speaker Ralston's Mental Health Parity Act (HB 1013) through his committee, which passed it unanimously; he argued police calls about suicide threats are 'more of a mental health issue' than a crime-enforcement one.
A legislative tracking site lists him as a joint (Senate) sponsor of HB 428 (2025, enacted), which codifies a right to in vitro fertilization in Georgia law.

Listed among the sponsors of SB 1, the 'Fair and Safe Athletic Opportunities Act' (2025, enacted), which restricts participation in girls' and women's school sports by sex at birth, according to a legislative tracking site.
Prioritizes representing Georgia’s coastal community interests.

people.background: Republican state senator for District 32 (East Cobb and part of Cherokee County) since winning a May 2017 special-election runoff. A retired orthopedic surgeon who practiced in metro Atlanta for more than 30 years and is a former president of Resurgens Orthopaedics; bachelor's degree, University of Kentucky (1976), M.D., University of Louisville (1980); age 71; born in Birmingham, Ala.; lives in East Cobb. people.ideology: Establishment-wing Republican who cites 'a conservative voting record': a physician-legislator focused on health care, insurance, children's services and veterans; endorsed by Gov. Brian Kemp in 2024 and says she 'proudly back[s] the blue.' No Freedom Caucus ties found.

positions.stance: Says she has voted for the gas-tax suspension, income-tax cuts, property-tax cuts and taxpayer rebates, which she credits to conservative fiscal management; supports capping property-tax increases so residents are not taxed out of their homes (2026).

Says she regularly works on insurance issues 'since they are directly related to healthcare'; her campaign site lists her health bills as covering transparency for consumers, surprise billing, emergency prescriptions and access to care across state lines including telemedicine, and says she carried legislation to improve Georgia's maternal-mortality statistics. As Children and Families chair, sponsored SB 431 (2026) requiring school districts to comply with enrollment requirements for children in foster care and SR 622 (2026) creating a joint study committee on escalating foster-care costs; sponsored SB 110 (2025, enacted) revising the Juvenile Code definition of neglect and SB 123 (2025, enacted) updating compulsory-attendance law.

Top priority is supporting service members, veterans and first responders; wants Georgia to be 'the most veteran-friendly state in the country'; advocated for a Veterans Education Career Transition Resource Center in Cobb County; sponsored SB 109 (2025, enacted) barring group life-insurance exclusions for deaths on active duty and SB 11 (2025, introduced; no further action) on retirement credit for military service.

people.name: Darcy Castro
people.background: Democratic nominee for Senate District 37 (West Cobb, Acworth and Kennesaw area plus part of Bartow County), leading incumbent Ed Setzler in the November count. people.name: Ed Setzler
people.background: Republican state senator for District 37 since January 2023, after 18 years in the Georgia House (District 35, northern Cobb, 2005-2023). Age 56; born in Atlanta; B.S. in physics, Furman University (1992), where he was a Distinguished Military Graduate; commissioned in 1992, he served nine years as a Regular Army officer (Ranger School graduate) and finished as commander of a 3rd Infantry Division truck transportation company at Fort Stewart. A registered architect and managing principal at St John Consulting Group; lives in Acworth. Chairs the Senate Science and Technology Committee and is vice chair of State and Local Governmental Operations (2025-2026); chaired the House Science and Technology Committee for most of 2013-2022. Unopposed in the 2026 GOP primary; trailing Democrat Darcy Castro in the November count.
people.ideology: Social-conservative Republican and one of the Legislature's leading anti-abortion and religious-liberty figures: lead sponsor of HB 481, the 2019 six-week abortion law, and main sponsor of SB 36, the 2025 religious-freedom bill; also emphasizes 'secure and verifiable' paper-backed ballots, income-tax reduction and school choice.

positions.stance: Lead sponsor of HB 481 (2019), a six-week abortion ban that Gov. Kemp signed in May 2019 and that took effect in 2022 after federal courts lifted an injunction following the Dobbs decision; his campaign bio lists 'the sanctity of human life' among the basic human rights he defends.

Main sponsor of SB 36, the Georgia Religious Freedom Restoration Act (2025), which he says mirrors the federal RFRA and shields people against state intrusion into their religious beliefs and practices; he resisted attempts to add language balancing religious claims against anti-discrimination protections. The bill passed and Gov. Kemp signed it in April 2025.

Supports expanding Medicaid to at-risk adults only with 'a 20-hour per week work mandate as a condition of receiving taxpayer funded healthcare'; supported HB 47 (buying health insurance across state lines), Haleigh's Hope Act (low-THC oil) and constitutionally protected trauma-care funding; helped negotiate expanded scope of practice for APRNs and PAs under physician supervision. Opposes legalizing recreational marijuana.
Supports continuing to reduce the state income tax (May 2026).
Says he believes in local control but that citizens, not county officials, should decide how they exercise the right to keep and bear arms (May 2026).

Says it is 'essential that we provide each voter with a ballot that is secure and verifiable'; as House Science and Technology chair he led a bipartisan review of new voting systems and sponsored a bipartisan bill that his site says 'laid the groundwork for requiring a paper-verifiable statewide election system'; says he helped pass SB 202.

Says he played 'a key leadership role' in school-choice options for special-needs families, HB 251 (intra-district transfers) and HR 1162 (the public charter-schools referendum), and that he 'fully funded the QBE funding formula'; a tracking site lists him among sponsors of SB 152 (2025) expanding Georgia Promise Scholarship eligibility to children of certain foster parents.

Says that as Science and Technology chair he helped lead passage of SB 219, which he calls 'the nation's premier driverless vehicle law,' and that he focuses on protecting children from AI harms; his campaign page has a data-centers heading but states no position.
Co-sponsored SB 390 (2024), which would withhold state funding from Georgia libraries affiliated with the American Library Association.

Listed among sponsors of SB 116 (2025, referred to committee) requiring DNA collection from people in detention facilities who are subject to immigration detainers, according to a legislative tracking site.

Votes to eliminate state income tax on family income up to $100,000/year and end taxpayer subsidies to datacenters, fought against corporate cronyism shifting tax burden to working families, opposed tax breaks for data centers and their cost shifting to residential rate payers, supported tax incentive to reduce traffic congestion by promoting tele-working.
q: Senator Ed Setzler votes to eliminate state income tax on family income up to $100,000/year and end taxpayer subsidies to datacenters.
Ed has consistently fought against “corporate cronyism” that shifts the state’s tax burden to working families.

positions.stance: Supported bipartisan ethics reform House Bill 5, supported Senate Bill 300, helped define addictive design and supported property rights legislation in response to Kelo vs. New London decision.

To provide an unprecedented level of transparency and accountability in state government agencies, Ed supported Senate Bill 300, the Transparency in Government Act, which publicizes state expenditures, contracts, audits, salaries, and travel expenses for every state agency and employee on a publicly

positions.stance: Supported tax incentive to reduce traffic congestion and promote tele-working; prioritized state spending to fund traffic relief and gave local governments more options to fund traffic relief; cast deciding vote in passage of Senate Bill 200 creating statewide Planning Director to prioritize mobility projects.
q: Ed supported a thoughtful tax incentive to reduce traffic congestion and promote tele-working.

As a former member of the House of Representatives, Ed has provided leadership in prioritizing state spending to fund much needed traffic relief and giving local governments more options to fund traffic relief at the local level.

positions.stance: Fought to protect local ordinances encouraging smart sustainable growth and vulnerable water wildlife resources, championed protecting greenspace and low-density residential character of West Cobb, supported creation of a Statewide Water Management Plan.
q: Ed has been recognized by Georgia Conservation Voters for his successful fight to protect local ordinances that encourage the smart, sustainable growth of our communities and for being instrumental in the protection of vulnerable water and wildlife resources statewide.
Ed has been a champion of protecting greenspace and protecting the low-density residential character of West Cobb.

positions.stance: Led bipartisan effort to protect freedom of assembly and protest, provided law enforcement tools against domestic terrorism and is recognized statewide leader in protecting due process, personal privacy, free speech, self-defense, education and sanctity of human life.
q: Ed led a bipartisan, multi-racial effort to protect the freedom of assembly and protest in Georgia, receiving a bipartisan award from Asian Americans Advancing Justice in Atlanta while providing law enforcement the tools to crack down on true cases of domestic terrorism.
Ed led a bipartisan, multi-racial effort to protect the freedom of assembly and protest in Georgia, receiving an award from Asian Americans Advancing Justice in Atlanta.

positions.stance: Has been active in criminal justice reform legislation for over a decade and worked to protect fundamental rights while providing law enforcement legitimate tools.
q: As a former member of the House Judiciary Noncivil Committee, Ed has played an active role in the debate and passage of virtually every piece of criminal justice reform legislation passed in Georgia for more than a decade.

As the former Chairman of the General Law Subcommittee of House Judiciary Noncivil, Ed has worked tirelessly to protect the fundamental rights of Georgians while providing law enforcement officials with the legitimate tools they need to protect Georgia’s communities.

positions.stance: Supports effective law enforcement and protecting constitutional liberties, supported increased funding for public safety, crack down on gangs and sexual exploitation of children.
q: Ed recognizes that effective law enforcement is essential to keeping Georgians secure and balances that belief with the recognition that protecting citizens’ constitutional liberties is essential to preserving a free society.

As violent protests broke out across the nation and the Left was demanding to “defund the police”, Ed stood up for law enforcement, helped secure increased funding for public safety, and crack down on the criminal street gangs and the sexual exploitation of children.

people.name: Kasey Carpenter
people.background: Republican state representative for House District 4 (Dalton, Whitfield County) since winning a November 2017 special election; a Dalton restaurant owner with a finance degree from the University of Georgia. Chairs the House Creative Arts & Entertainment Committee (named January 2023) and sits on Appropriations, Ways and Means, Higher Education, Transportation, Regulated Industries and Industry and Labor. Won the May 2026 Republican primary over Cleve Manis 65.9%-34.1%. In April 2026 he apologized for a party photo taken more than a decade earlier in which he wore blackface while dressed as Kanye West, saying, 'That position missed the mark for many. For that I apologize.'
people.ideology: Republican who has broken with his party on immigration: the only House Republican to vote against the 2024 Georgia Criminal Alien Track and Report Act (HB 1105), for which the Whitfield County GOP (March 2024, also citing his support for a Patterson Farms tax allocation district) and the 14th Congressional District GOP (May 2024) censured him; has pushed for in-state tuition for DACA recipients (Dalton Daily Citizen, May 2024; AJC, May 2025).

positions.stance: Was the only House Republican to vote against the Georgia Criminal Alien Track and Report Act (HB 1105, 2024), which requires local law enforcement to cooperate with federal immigration authorities. He said, 'I think we ought to support our sheriffs and police officers, not penalize them for not being immigration experts,' and, noting that his district is 52% minority, said Hispanics and other people of color could be profiled.

After Ximena Arias-Cristobal was arrested by a Dalton police officer after a traffic stop and turned over to federal immigration authorities (May 2025), he wrote a character letter calling her 'a person of high moral character' and launched a Change.org petition asking Congress to overhaul the immigration system, combining tighter border security with a pathway to citizenship for some immigrants living in the U.S. without legal status: 'I am sick and tired of everyone kicking the can on immigration and only focusing on one aspect.'
Over the years has pushed to allow young immigrants protected under DACA to pay in-state tuition (AJC, May 2025).
Sponsored HB 328 (2026), raising the annual aggregate cap on tax credits for contributions to student scholarship organizations (private-school scholarships); signed into law May 11, 2026.

Sponsored HB 1164 (2026), requiring the State Board of Education to appoint an audit committee (signed May 12, 2026), and HB 1293 (2026), updating eligibility for the Dual Achievement Program (signed May 5, 2026).

people.record: Sole House Republican 'no' vote on HB 1105 (2024). Chairs Creative Arts & Entertainment since 2023. 2025-26 bills that became law: HB 328 (student scholarship organization tax-credit cap), HB 455 (bingo sessions), HB 1164 (State Board of Education audit committee), HB 1293 (Dual Achievement Program); HB 14 (designating cornbread the official state bread) was vetoed May 12, 2026.

people.name: Joseph Gullett
people.background: Republican state representative for House District 19 (Dallas; Paulding and Cobb counties) since January 2019. Technology professional, age 46 (May 2026), born in Gwinnett County (Norcross), with a B.S. in applied computer science from Columbus State University. Former chairman of the Paulding County Republican Party and board member of the Paulding County Boys & Girls Club. Serves on Appropriations, Banks and Banking, Governmental Affairs, Insurance, Judiciary Juvenile, Judiciary Non-Civil and Technology and Infrastructure Innovation. Unopposed in the 2026 Republican primary (6,038 votes).
people.ideology: Conservative Republican who calls himself the 'Conservative Workhorse' and is a former Paulding County GOP chair; campaigns on tax cuts (goal of a zero percent income tax), housing affordability and insurance costs; listed on Georgia Chamber, NFIB, Club for Growth and Freedom Index scorecards (scores not shown).

positions.stance: Says that when the state has a surplus 'that money belongs to the people, not the government,' citing nearly $12 billion returned to taxpayers since he was first elected (a temporary gas-tax suspension, income-tax rebates, and a homeowner tax relief grant saving homesteaded owners around $500); supports 'continued and responsible reduction of the state income tax with the goal of moving toward a zero percent rate' and capping annual assessment increases at the rate of inflation (MDJ, May 2026).

Names housing affordability as a top issue, pledging to keep homeownership attainable by 'fighting corporate overreach in our residential markets'; also names consumer insurance relief, 'championing transparency and market reforms to drive down the cost of insurance for every household.'

Says he typically defers to local leaders and believes in local control as a general rule, but will step in when necessary to ensure consistency, uphold the rule of law or protect the interests and liberties of taxpayers.

Sponsored HB 447 (2026), creating crimes of gift-card theft, forgery and fraud, and HB 1075 (2026), increasing penalties for repeat offenders convicted of trafficking persons for labor or sexual servitude; both signed May 12, 2026.
Sponsored HB 256 (2026), revising the foster parents' bill of rights; signed May 11, 2026.
Sponsored HB 304 (2026), creating the Georgia Municipal Court Clerks' Council, and HB 1587 (2026), abolishing the elected Cobb County surveyor in favor of appointment; both signed May 2026.

Believes budget should reflect commitment to education, infrastructure, and public safety; believes teachers shape society through commitment to students' growth and development; supports providing educators with tools, support, and autonomy to succeed in classroom.
q: Our budget should reflect our commitment to education, infrastructure, and public safety.
Teachers shape the future of our society with their commitment to our students' growth and development.

positions.stance: Supports legislation encouraging entrepreneurship, reducing regulations, and keeping taxes low, says legislators should ease access, streamline bureaucracy, and promote patient choice, says will fight for policies that foster competition, innovation, drive down costs, and expand options, says easing tax and regulation burden on small businesses can help them grow and expand.
q: I work hard to continue cultivating this fertile soil by enacting legislation that encourages entrepreneurship, reduces excessive regulations, and keeps taxes low I support policies that empower individuals to pursue education and training that align with the demands of a rapidly evolving job market
As legislators, our focus should be on easing access, streamlining bureaucracy, and promoting patient choice.

positions.stance: Supports policies addressing victims' rights, root causes of crime, and evolving criminal offenses, supports initiatives fostering positive relationships between citizens and law enforcement, and supports effective crime prevention through mutual trust and understanding.
q: I support policies that address victims’ rights, the root causes of crime, and the evolving nature of criminal offenses in our interconnected world.
That’s why I support initiatives that help foster positive relationships between citizens and law enforcement officers.

positions.stance: Supports equipping individuals to make their own health care choices.
q: I believe in equipping individuals to make their own health care choices.

people.background: Ran as a Republican in the partisan races on record. Won the race for State House District 20 in 2020, 2022 (unopposed) and 2024 (unopposed). Her platform calls for eliminating the income tax, hand-marked paper ballots, ending 'the Woke Agenda' and 'medical freedom.'

people.background: Ran as a Democrat in the partisan races on record. In the November 3, 2026 general election (count not yet certified), trailed in the race for State House District 21.

positions.stance: Believes competition, accountability, and representation are important, says representatives should represent real people, says every agency should explain its authority, says the gap between promises and results is widening, and believes state action should require transparency and constitutional compliance.
