The goal is to represent real people faithfully, especially when party comfort pushes against local accountability.

positions.stance: Says Georgia can require constitutional compliance, demand transparency, and defend residents from unlawful detention and search; says a representative should not talk down to people or hide behind talking points; says no agency should enter a home without a judicial warrant.

A representative should not talk down to people or hide behind talking points.

q: Georgia can support public safety while still insisting that every level of government follow constitutional limits.
If you care about lower costs, local accountability, and enforcing constitutional limits, start here.

positions.stance: Believes representatives should answer to people, not party pressure.
q: Whether the issue is taxes, schools, healthcare, public safety, or federal enforcement, Anthony believes representatives should answer to the people here, not party pressure in Atlanta or Washington.

positions.stance: Says families deserve lower costs, honest information, and a government that follows the Constitution.
q: I'm running because families deserve lower costs, honest information, and a government that follows the Constitution even when politics gets loud.

people.name: Jordan Ridley
people.background: Republican state representative for House District 22 (Woodstock; Cherokee and Cobb counties) since January 2023, elected in 2022 and re-elected in 2024 over James Shade 60.5%-39.5%. A Cherokee County native (campaign site) with a bachelor's in public policy from Georgia State University; the Cherokee Tribune's April 2026 voter guide lists him as a business owner, age 34. Vice chair of the Code Revision Committee; serves on Energy, Utilities and Telecommunications; Game, Fish and Parks; and Public Safety and Homeland Security. Unopposed in the 2026 Republican primary (5,618 votes).
people.ideology: Conservative Republican whose campaign says he 'fights for smaller government, low taxes, and the future our families deserve'; campaign issue headings include 'Protecting Parental Rights,' 'Expanding Educational Opportunity' and 'Defending Constitutional Freedoms.'

positions.stance: Co-introduced HB 33EX with Rep. Charlice Byrd in the June 2026 special session to provide a homestead exemption from Cherokee County ad valorem taxes; his campaign says he fights for 'low taxes.' The Cherokee Tribune guide (April 2026) reports he named affordability and taxes as residents' greatest challenge.
Sponsored HB 967 (2026) to fund bullet-resistant equipment for law-enforcement vehicles; praised its House passage in March 2026.
Sponsored HB 845 to establish an internal auditor for the Cherokee County Board of Education; it passed the House (campaign site).
Sponsors the 'Justice for Peanut and Fred Act,' aimed at preventing hasty decisions by authorities and ensuring animals are treated fairly.
Joined a July 2026 joint statement by Cherokee-area House Republicans responding to Holly Springs' lawsuit over de-annexation following enactment of HB 1029.
Appointed in May 2026 to the House Blue-Ribbon Study Committee on Youth Exposure to Kratom and Retail-Available Substances.

Recognizes healthcare costs are skyrocketing, and hospitals are closing, creating a crisis that must be addressed; committed to finding creative solutions to streamline payment processes and make healthcare costs transparent and understandable; will work to protect independent pharmacies, reduce prescription costs, ensure access to quality healthcare in rural areas and uphold medical freedom.
q: $$I recognize that healthcare costs are skyrocketing, and hospitals are closing, creating a crisis that we must address.
I am committed to finding creative solutions to streamline payment processes and make healthcare costs transparent and understandable.

The proposed "Justice for Peanut and Fred Act," seeks to ensure that Georgia’s pet owners and their pets are protected from such blatant government overreach.

positions.stance: Has been a reliable conservative vote fighting to reduce government overreach, defend the Second Amendment, protect taxpayers, strengthen local control, and uphold values; supports stronger laws to protect vulnerable individuals from sex trafficking.

The fight against sex trafficking is crucial, and I will advocate for stronger laws to protect our most vulnerable.

positions.stance: Would defend the Second Amendment, safeguarding every citizen's fundamental right to bear arms.

It's crucial for local communities to have the autonomy to determine their own futures without directives from higher levels

positions.stance: Believes state should cut red tape, maintain low taxes, and support business growth.
q: I am dedicated to ensuring our state continues to cut unnecessary red tape, maintain low taxes, and remain an excellent place for businesses to thrive.

q: I voted to protect women in women’s sports because it’s essential to preserve the spaces where females can compete fairly and safely.

people.name: Michelle Kang
people.background: Community organizer and former small-business owner from Gwinnett County; a first-generation Korean American born in Incheon who came to Georgia in 1992. She holds a master's in public administration from the University of Georgia (2009), worked earlier as a paralegal in Seoul, managed the Asian American Resource Center and organized for Sen. Raphael Warnock's 2022 campaign. In 2024 she lost House District 99 to Rep. Matt Reeves by 621 votes (48.9%-51.1%); in 2026 she won the Democratic primary with 71.5% over Shelly Abraham.
people.ideology: Progressive Democrat: endorsed by the Working Families Party and GA WIN List (2024) and Next Gen Politics and Way to Lead (2026); calls for higher taxes on the top 1% and universal childcare.

positions.stance: Supports repealing Georgia's six-week abortion ban; says women's health decisions 'should be protected' in consultation with their doctors (2024 survey; 2024 AJC).
Would cut income taxes for families earning $100,000 or less, expand the Earned Income Tax Credit and childcare credits, and raise taxes on the top 1% (individuals earning over $586,000).
Calls universal childcare 'central to the affordability of life in Georgia'; would build on free Pre-K to cover children under 6.

Supports allowing accessory dwelling units by right, limiting corporate purchases of homes, state habitability standards for rentals, renter protections against unfair rent hikes, and a solar rebate program.
Says she will 'expand Medicaid' and 'rein in health insurance companies'; 'No Georgian should have to decide between a medical bill and their power bill.'
Would fully fund the QBE formula, raise teacher pay, add special-needs and mental-health support and reduce class sizes.
Signed a 2024 pledge supporting safe-storage laws, universal background checks and red-flag laws.
Would expand access to capital, fund apprenticeships, cut licensing barriers and prioritize Georgia businesses for state contracts.

As your representative, and as a first-generation Korean American immigrant, I will:; stand up to anti-immigrant legislation and ensure Georgia never targets families for political gain; push for expanded language access in schools, healthcare, and public services.

people.name: Matt Reeves
people.background: Two-term Republican state representative (elected 2022, re-elected 2024 with 51.1%) and real estate and business litigation partner at Andersen, Tate & Carr in Duluth. A native of Americus who grew up in Jacksonville, Fla., he graduated with honors from Mercer University and UGA School of Law and has lived in Gwinnett since 2003; he is a past president of the Gwinnett County Bar Association and Duluth Rotary and served on the Duluth parks board. He lost state Senate District 48 races in 2018 and 2020. In the House he is vice chair of the Judiciary Committee, secretary of Reapportionment and Redistricting, a member of Appropriations and Insurance, and on the Majority Caucus whip team.
people.ideology: Mainstream business-wing Republican in the House leadership orbit: majority whip team, Georgia Chamber-scored, endorsed by Educators First, ranked 4th most effective House member by the Center for Effective Lawmaking; the AJC reported he kept his distance from the 2024 Trump campaign.

positions.stance: Sponsored HB 1074 (2026) authorizing a November 2026 referendum on a $15,000 Suwanee homestead exemption; sponsored a 2024 Gwinnett homeowner property-tax cut that passed with 75% at referendum; in 2020 called for cutting the state income tax and capping spending.
Co-sponsored a gun safe-storage tax credit bill that stalled in the Senate in 2024 and said he planned to reintroduce it.
Said in 2024 he would follow how the appellate courts handle Georgia's six-week law rather than stake out a new position.

Sponsored HB 1020 (2026) raising district attorney pay and updating the Judicial Retirement System, signed by Gov. Kemp; co-sponsored HB 304 (2026) creating a senior municipal court judge office, for which the Council of Municipal Court Judges gave him a perseverance award.
Sponsored HB 1247 and HB 1254 (2026), described as reforms to state regulatory systems, both signed into law in May 2026.
Serves as Gwinnett County Public Schools liaison for the caucus; endorsed by Educators First; in 2020 favored keeping the HOPE grant merit-based.
Kept distance from Donald Trump's 2024 campaign and framed suburban Atlanta as 'the battleground,' focusing on local issues (AJC, Oct. 2024).
Co-hosted a Gwinnett mental health workshop with Suwanee officials and the DBHDD commissioner in September 2026.
Says he 'believes in the value of Live-Work-Play communities' and campaigns as 'Fighting for Gwinnett's Taxpayers.'

people.record: 2025-2026: sponsored HB 1020 (DA pay/judicial retirement), HB 1247 and HB 1254 (regulatory reform) and HB 1074 (Suwanee homestead referendum), all enacted; co-sponsored HB 304 (municipal courts). 2023-2024: Gwinnett homeowner property-tax cut approved by voters; ranked 4th of 180 House members and 1st among freshmen for legislative effectiveness (Center for Effective Lawmaking, April 2025); named Georgia Credit Union Association's 2024 lawmaker of the year.

positions.stance: Supports economic growth and small business; opposes data centers as long-term job engines; supports responsible growth that brings opportunities and jobs while protecting natural character.

people.name: Carolyn F. Hugley
people.background: Columbus Democrat elected to the Georgia House in 1992 (serving since 1993), first in District 136 and since January 2023 in District 141. House Minority Leader since January 13, 2025, elected by the House Democratic Caucus on Nov. 14, 2024; her campaign site says she was the first African American Minority Whip of the Georgia House (2003-2018). A longtime State Farm insurance agent; B.A. in political science from the University of Arkansas at Pine Bluff and M.P.A. from Mississippi State University; born in Forrest City, Arkansas. Serves on Appropriations, Banks and Banking, Ethics, Insurance, Rules and Urban Affairs. On Nov. 4, 2026 the AJC reported Democrats led in enough seats to win the House if results hold, putting her in line to potentially become the first Black woman Speaker of the Georgia House.
people.ideology: Mainstream Democratic leader of the House Democratic Caucus, whose 2026 'Live, Learn, Earn' agenda includes a higher minimum wage, PeachCare for adults and need-based HOPE; has also worked with Republicans, co-sponsoring the sports-betting amendment HR 450.

positions.stance: In a December 2024 interview she called the failure to expand Medicaid the most egregious Republican policy, citing poor enrollment in Gov. Kemp's Pathways program, 12% of Georgians uninsured and nine rural hospital closures.
Her caucus 'Opportunity Agenda' for 2025 focused on economic attainment, educational advancement and healthy, sustainable communities so people 'not just survive, but to thrive.'

Said in December 2024 she would not be surprised by new abortion or contraception restrictions, more likely in an election year, and that the best response is electing more members who prioritize reproductive freedom.

Co-sponsored HR 450, a proposed constitutional amendment letting the legislature legalize sports betting with proceeds for education and addiction programs; it failed on the House floor 63-98 on March 6, 2026 (120 votes needed).
Named the budget, gaming, child welfare, infrastructure and Hurricane Helene recovery as areas for bipartisan work (December 2024).

The caucus she leads outlined a 2026 agenda to raise the minimum wage, give tax cuts to employers paying livable wages, extend PeachCare to adults, restore need-based HOPE, limit corporate ownership of homes, and pursue safe-storage and red-flag gun measures (WSB, October 2025; the article quotes caucus chair Tanya Miller, not Hugley).
Her campaign site says she focuses on issues affecting Georgia's children and families and on fighting for 'the everyday Georgian.'

people.record: House Minority Leader since Jan. 13, 2025; Minority Whip 2003-2018 (per her campaign site). Co-sponsored HR 450, the sports-betting constitutional amendment that failed 63-98 on March 6, 2026.

signals.claim: If Democrats' Nov. 4 leads hold, likely to be the Democratic nominee for Speaker and to advance the caucus agenda (minimum wage increase, PeachCare for adults, need-based HOPE).

positions.stance: Allocates critical funding to rebuild communities affected by the storm; addresses urgent need to provide relief for Georgians impacted by Hurricane Helene; prioritizes recovery efforts following Hurricane Helene.
q: The storm’s widespread destruction prompted an urgent need for recovery, and this budget allocates critical funding to help rebuild affected communities.
One of the most critical areas addressed in the House’s version of the amended budget is the urgent need to provide relief for Georgians impacted by Hurricane Helene.

positions.stance: Supports HB 123 allowing life in prison instead of death penalty if defendant has ID; supports legislation targeting human trafficking with bipartisan support.
q: Under HB 123, if the court finds the defendant does have an ID, the jury could choose to sentence that individual to life in prison instead of the death penalty.

As one of the Kemp Administration’s top priorities and building on the work of the GRACE Commission—led by First Lady Marty Kemp—the Georgia General Assembly has passed ten pieces of legislation targeting human trafficking.

positions.stance: Requires insurers to lower prior authorization requirements for high-performing providers and requires insurance commissioner to submit a report outlining implementation of coverage requirement.
q: We and our House colleagues also gave final passage to Senate Bill 5, which outlines requirements for insurers regarding prior authorization programs, mandating that they lower prior authorization requirements for high-performing providers.

Additionally, the bill requires the insurance commissioner submit a report by July 1, 2032, to the House Insurance Committee and the Senate Insurance and Labor Committee, outlining the implementation of this coverage requirement.

positions.stance: Highlighting impact of AI on legal system and forming committee to assess findings.
q: He also highlighted that Georgia courts are proactively examining the impact of generative artificial intelligence (AI) on our legal system and have formed a committee to assess their findings and discover what challenges or opportunities could come from the use of AI in the judicial system.

positions.stance: Proposed $1.8 billion for McDonough Area I-75 Henry County Express Lanes.
q: He also proposed major transportation projects, including $1.8 billion for the always congested McDonough Area at I-75 Henry County Express Lanes; $250 million for local roads and $100 million for rural bridge improvements.

positions.stance: Supports HB 266 to support Georgia’s military veterans.
q: House Bill 266, supports Georgia’s military veterans, also received final passage and is now awaiting the governor’s decision.
